payload.text: Siggy has raised $6 million in pre-seed funding to build a mental health service that uses AI to collect patients’ histories and track progress between appointments with licensed clinicians, the startup told Crunchbase News exclusively. The company brings together two founders who previously built businesses that help patients get treatment outside a traditional doctor’s office. Jonathan Sabbagh co-founded Journey Clinical , which supports practices offering ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and Edvard Engesæth co-founded Nurx , which provides birth control and other healthcare services online. Village Global led the financing for New York-based Siggy. Notably, several investors in the round previously backed one or both founders. They include Albert Wenger of Union Square Ventures , Mercury co-founder Immad Akhund , and Cityblock Health co-founder Toyin Ajayi , through Coalition Operators . Other participants include PsyMed Ventures , Mystic Ventures and Gokul Rajaram . Jonathan Sabbagh and Edvard Engesæth, co-founders of Siggy. (Courtesy photo) The founders said they began building Siggy in late 2025. The round, which they plan to use to hire more clinicians and engineers, develop the software and work on regulatory requirements, is the first outside funding for the company. The startup recently began accepting paying patients ahead of its public launch, and the founders said they next plan to test the service with paying patients before expanding further. Between appointments Sabbagh, Siggy’s CEO, told Crunchbase News in an interview that the company is addressing a problem he encountered in mental healthcare. Therapists and the clinicians prescribing their patients’ medication often work separately. Patients may see a therapist weekly but have only a brief appointment every few months with their prescriber. This leaves little time or opportunity to discuss changes in symptoms or medication side effects. To address that problem, Siggy uses AI conversations and daily check-ins to gather information clinicians can review between visits. “AI helps maintain the conversation and organize what patients share, so clinicians have a richer picture of the person that they’re treating,” said Engesæth, the startup’s COO, in an interview. Patients begin by answering questions about their history through a free AI conversation. They then meet a licensed clinician by video, who reviews that information. The clinician then makes a diagnosis and prescribes medication if appropriate. Patients can talk with Siggy’s AI between appointments and can also check in each day to report their sleep, mood, medication and how they feel physically. The company combines those answers with data from connected wearable devices to produce a daily “Siggy Score” out of 100. The score is visible to both the patient and clinician. Patients can opt to connect wearables such as Whoop , Oura or Apple Watch, adding sleep, activity, heart rate and heart rate variability data to the daily check-ins that underpin the Siggy Score. The company aims to use those patterns to flag difficult stretches earlier, including when patients report feeling fine despite worsening sleep or other physical changes. If the score changes, the software flags it for a clinician to review. Patients also receive weekly check-ins during their first eight weeks of treatment, according to the company. Clinicians decide whether to continue treatment or adjust medication, and also handle all medical questions. When appropriate, they can help patients taper off gradually. Siggy does not prescribe controlled substances and is not a crisis service, the founders said. One important note: Patients can continue seeing their existing therapists while using Siggy, Sabbagh said. A planned feature would let patients share information with other providers and involve loved ones in their care. A prior working relationship As with many startup founders, Sabbagh’s interest in mental health treatment grew out of his own experience. After two decades in finance, he experienced burnout and was eventually diagnosed with PTSD related to childhood trauma. He said ketamine-assisted therapy helped him recover, leading him to return to school to study psychology at 38. He subsequently co-founded Journey Clinical. Sabbagh said he has since become its executive chairman, remaining involved while taking on the CEO role at Siggy. Engesæth, a physician by training, was an early investor in Journey and advised Sabbagh as he built the company. Before that, Engesæth co-founded Nurx, which initially helped patients obtain birth control prescriptions and receive medication at home. He said the company grew to more than 2 million patients and an annual revenue run rate exceeding $100 million before merging with Thirty Madison in 2022. The two had considered starting a company together for years. With Siggy, they say they want to make the regular contact and coordination Sabbagh had with his own providers available to more patients. Accepting insurance Siggy accepts commercial insurance in all 50 states and is expanding into government insurance programs. Patients can also pay directly; insured patients’ costs vary by plan. Insurance was a priority because many prospective patients cannot afford treatment out of pocket, Engesæth said. The founders also say Siggy’s service will be permanently free to veterans. Investor POV Amrit Rao , a general partner at Village Global, told Crunchbase News via email that the founders’ experience building healthcare companies was a major reason he invested. The fact that Siggy accepts insurance was important too. “Pairing that vision with an insurance-based model makes the ambition about access as much as technology,” he said. Mercury co-founder and CEO Immad Akhund, who invested personally, is a repeat backer of both founders.  He pointed to their longer-term ambition of using AI to understand each patient’s brain health well enough to detect changes early. “That’s why I’m backing them again with Siggy,” he added, “and why I’m excited to be in early on what they build next.” Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To AI Healthcare Companies In 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Dropbox announced Thursday plans to acquire Tigris Data for $350 million in a transaction the company told Crunchbase News would mark its largest acquisition since its founding in 2007. Founded by former Uber engineers, Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris is building a network of localized data storage centers that it claims can meet the distributed compute needs of modern AI workloads. Tigris has raised about $31.9 million since its founding in 2021, per Crunchbase data . Its October 2025 Series A brought in $25 million from lead investor Spark Capital , with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and Basis Set Ventures , which also led its seed round. Other earlier backers include General Catalyst . Co-founder and CEO Ovais Tariq told TechCrunch at the time of its Series A that the startup had grown 8x every year since its founding in November 2021. The planned deal would give Dropbox a storage platform built for developers whose applications run across multiple cloud providers. A push into AI infrastructure The acquisition news coincides with what San Francisco-based Dropbox describes as “a significant shift” in its AI strategy as it expands beyond storing and sharing files into selling the infrastructure that companies use to build AI applications. Publicly traded Dropbox also unveiled DBX Agent Cloud, which will initially offer standalone object storage —  a way to store and retrieve large collections of data, including images, video and the files used to train and run AI models. For Dropbox, buying Tigris offers a faster route into a market that serves a different audience from the individuals and businesses that use its file-sharing software. “Tigris brings together a product already running in production, an experienced team, and established relationships with AI developers,” Eric Webster , Dropbox’s chief business officer, told Crunchbase News via email. “That combination would accelerate our entry into infrastructure for AI applications through DBX Agent Cloud.” A bigger bet amid a slower deal pace Dropbox has made 35 known acquisitions, according to Crunchbase, with much of that activity taking place in its earlier years. Between 2012 and 2015, the company conducted 23 publicly reported acquisitions, including nine in 2014 alone. In contrast, it made four acquisitions across 2024 and 2025, averaging two per year, roughly 65% below its earlier pace. Its recent purchases suggest a focus on AI-powered productivity, search and security. Dropbox acquired scheduling startup Reclaim.ai and document security company Nira in 2024, followed by Promoted.ai and Mobius Labs in 2025. While the planned Tigris purchase would be its largest yet, Dropbox has made other sizable purchases over time. Its acquisitions of e-signature company HelloSign in 2019, document-sharing platform DocSend in 2021 and business forms provider FormSwift in 2022 had purchase prices of $230 million, $165 million and $95 million, respectively. Two paths into AI Dropbox’s push into AI infrastructure is one part of a broader strategy that also includes adding AI capabilities to its existing file-sharing product. For existing customers, the company is bringing AI directly to their Dropbox files to help them find, understand, create, edit and organize content, according to Webster. Customers can switch between supported AI models and work with their Dropbox files in tools like ChatGPT and Claude, with results returning to Dropbox. For companies and developers, meanwhile, DBX Agent Cloud extends Dropbox’s storage capabilities to the infrastructure behind AI applications and agents. “DBX Agent Cloud opens a new developer and infrastructure market for Dropbox, while AI inside Dropbox is intended to deepen engagement, retention and expansion among existing customers,” Webster said. payload.text: Construction companies are struggling to find enough workers. For startups, that means venture investors are pouring money into companies betting that robots can help close the gap. Companies spanning construction and robotics have raised about $1.6 billion this year through Oct. 29 — more than 4x the $389 million recorded in all of 2025 — according to Crunchbase data. The surge was driven by three companies that raised the majority of the funding. The broad trend: For contractors struggling to hire, the appeal of construction-oriented tech offerings is straightforward: They need to get work done and there aren’t enough skilled workers to do it. The AI-driven data center building boom is only adding to that competition for workers. Labor shortages remain the biggest cause of project delays, according to a recent survey by the Associated General Contractors of America and NCCER . Some of the technology is already at work on job sites. San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics , this year’s largest funding recipient in the sector, said in August that excavators equipped with its autonomous systems were operating without human operators on commercial projects in Texas and Nevada. The numbers: With roughly two months left in the year, funding has already surpassed the previous five years combined. Companies spanning construction and robotics raised about $1.6 billion through Oct. 29, 3x the previous high of $506 million in 2021, according to our dataset that goes back to 2018. This year’s total is also more than 3x the 2021 high of $506 million. So far, the funding surge reflects much bigger bets rather than more deals. The sector has recorded 30 rounds this year, compared with 28 in all of 2025. Bedrock alone accounts for $870 million across two deals — more than half of this year’s total. This underscores just how much a few large financings are impacting the recovery. Austin-based Icon , which builds homes using 3D printing, also raised two rounds in 2026. It has raised nearly $800 million since its 2017 inception. A company spokesperson told Crunchbase News that the company has taken its technology from an experiment to “an in-the-field system that can build faster, with fewer people, less waste, greater design freedom and lower cost.” To date, the company has built more than 270 homes and structures across five states and two countries. It says that it’s on pace to grow revenue by 4x this year. “Early on, the question was whether a robotic construction system could build a good home,” the spokesperson wrote via email. “Today, the question is whether a company can deliver at volume, across geographies and project types, and improve its economics with each build. That’s only answerable with time in the field.” Notable deals Bedrock Robotics was the largest funding recipient in 2026, impressively raising $870 million across two rounds. The 2-year-old company, which converts existing heavy construction equipment into autonomous machines, announced a $600 million Series C in October led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital . That round, which valued Bedrock at $4.1 billion, followed a $270 million Series B in February led by CapitalG and Valor Atreides AI Fund . Austin-based construction technology company Icon also raised two rounds, bringing its listed 2026 funding to $265 million. Its largest financing was a $200 million Series D in October led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock , following a $65 million Series C in March. Another $200 million round went to Gravis Robotics , based in Zurich, Switzerland, which develops technology to retrofit construction machinery for autonomous earthmoving and excavation. SoftBank led the company’s Series A in August, which valued the startup at $1 billion post-money. Beyond those large financings, investors backed companies automating homebuilding and specific construction tasks. Reframe Systems , based in Andover, Massachusetts, uses AI, robotics and automation to build homes. It raised $40 million in an August venture round led by Energy Impact Partners . Amsterdam, Netherlands-based Monumental , developer of robots for on-site masonry and other building workflows, secured a $32 million Series B in July led by Khosla Ventures . Meanwhile Las Vegas-based August Robotics raised a $30 million Series B in May led by Big Pi Ventures . Its autonomous systems serve construction, exhibitions, industrial fit-out and facility operations. Belmont, California-based Gritt , which develops AI-powered robotic systems for infrastructure construction, followed with a $26 million Series A in July led by Obvious Ventures . Sizable seed rounds also made the list. London-based All3 , which uses AI and robotics to design, manufacture and assemble buildings, raised $25 million in April led by RTP Global . Origin , based in San Francisco, developing a general-purpose construction robot, secured $20 million in October, led by Accel and Zacua Ventures . Exits Acquisitions have dominated exit activity in construction robotics and related jobsite automation this year. One of the largest disclosed deals was Carpinteria, California-based Procore ’s acquisition of DroneDeploy , a San Francisco-based platform that combines imagery from drones, ground robots and cameras to track construction progress and site conditions. Procore announced the approximately $845 million cash transaction in July and closed it in September. Other buyers have focused on automating the work itself. In January, Oshkosh subsidiary JLG Industries acquired the core technology developed by Canvas , a San Francisco-based startup known for robotic drywall finishing. Heavy-equipment autonomy also attracted buyers. In March, HavocAI completed its acquisition of Palo Alto, California-based Teleo , whose technology lets operators remotely oversee heavy machinery. The following month, San Francisco-based Pronto confirmed that Atoms , Travis Kalanick ’s physical AI company, had completed its acquisition for an undisclosed price. Pronto’s autonomous haulage technology now reportedly underpins Atoms’ mining division. Public offerings have been less prominent, with no known IPOs this year by companies focused specifically on construction robotics. The broader construction technology market did produce a sizable debut: Columbia, Missouri-based EquipmentShare , an equipment rental and connected-jobsite technology company, raised approximately $747 million in gross proceeds in its January IPO, selling 30.5 million shares at $24.50 each. For all the variety in the companies attracting funding, this year’s surge has so far largely rested on three: Bedrock, Icon and Gravis, which together accounted for more than $1.3 billion, or about 83%, of the roughly $1.6 billion raised. Investors are placing unusually large bets on a small group of companies, even as acquisitions give others a route into larger businesses already serving construction customers. payload.text: For the past few decades, the vast majority of U.S. startup funding has consistently gone to companies in blue states or purple states, where Democrats control all or some statewide offices. But with Tuesday’s election results, the investment divide between blue, purple and red states has grown even more pronounced. So far this year, less than 2% of all startup investment has gone to companies in post-election red states, defined as those that will have both a Republican governor and two Republican U.S. senators. The red states’ share is much smaller than in years past due to five states shifting to purple. Of those, the largest venture hub is Texas, which shifted to purple with the election of Democratic Senator James Talarico and Governor Gina Hinojosa, followed by Ohio. This year, as of Election Day, startups in the remaining 17 red states 1 , which are home to nearly a quarter of Americans, had collectively pulled in just $8.6 billion in venture funding, with Florida, Tennessee and Utah among the largest contributors. To put that in perspective: It’s less than the typical nationwide total in a single week. Purple states rising The 10 purple U.S. states 2 , meanwhile, are home to just over a quarter of Americans and pulled in about $28.6 billion this year as of Election Day. That’s much higher than the red state tally, but still less than 6% of all U.S. startup funding. Beyond the aforementioned newcomers Texas and Ohio, several other purple states regularly pull in sizable venture funding, including Pennsylvania, North Carolina and to some extent Wisconsin. Also worth noting: The divide between red, purple and blue states is somewhat less stark when it comes to round counts. About 12% of startup financings of $1 million or more went to purple state companies this year, and about 9% went to red states. Broadly, it looks like backers are still finding plenty of investment-worthy talent outside of blue states when it comes to smaller deals. However, they are concentrating most of their capital into big AI rounds for California and New York companies. Blue states get over 90% of startup funding This brings us to our next point: Blue states receive the overwhelming majority of startup funding, of which most goes to California. 3 Per a Crunchbase analysis last week, California companies had pulled in more than three-fourths of all U.S. startup funding in 2026. Most of that stems from mega-financings for San Francisco-based OpenAI and Anthropic . While no other state comes close to California for attracting investment, the nearest runners up are also predominantly blue states, including New York and Massachusetts. In total, blue states have pulled in a staggering $481 billion in startup investment this year as of Election Day, per Crunchbase data, a new record. Politics and what makes for a venture hub So is it politics, or coincidence? Broadly speaking, the qualities that geographic startup hubs share — such as a deep tech talent pool, urban environs, leading tech companies and top research universities — aren’t specifically the domain of blue states. That said, predominantly rural states, which tend to lean red, are less likely to have those ingredients. Even so, there’s no rule against red state startup prowess. Austin, for example, managed to cement its status as a major tech hub even while Texas remained solidly under Republican control. And Utah also boasts a sophisticated startup scene. But following a Democratic electoral sweep, it’s hardly a surprise that more startup hubs now find themselves located in blue or purple states. payload.text: The majority of U.S. venture capital nowadays goes to companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires. This is not a difficult stat to unearth. So far this year, just seven companies raised more than half of all seed- through growth-stage investment. They’re mostly familiar names: OpenAI , Anthropic , xAI (now part of SpaceX ), Anduril Industries , Databricks , Prometheus and The Boring Co. These companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year. That’s just over 50% of the U.S. seed and venture investment over the same period, per Crunchbase data. Founders and CEOs of these seven companies are also well-known — and exceptionally  well-off to boot. The world’s wealthiest men Two founders are particularly famous. They are the world’s wealthiest men: Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos . Musk founded xAI and The Boring Co., and also co-founded OpenAI, (though he has no known equity stake in the latter). And while outside investors funded these companies, Musk could have also afforded to do so himself. Ditto for Bezos, who in 2025 launched the physical AI startup Prometheus, which raised $12 billion earlier this year. Bezos’ own net worth, meanwhile, is calculated at more than $350 billion. AI’s leading names The two highest valuation startups — OpenAI and the soon-to-be-public Anthropic — also have prominent billionaire founders and CEOs. However, they have mixed backstories to their wealth. OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman primarily made his vast wealth through investments in Y Combinator startups, including Stripe and Reddit . Altman has said he does not have an equity stake in OpenAI beyond a sliver from an old YC round. Co-founder Greg Brockman , by contrast, has a larger stake in OpenAI that was reportedly valued around $30 billion earlier this year. At Anthropic, meanwhile, all seven company co-founders have similar-sized equity stakes, and each is worth billions. This includes the AI giant’s most famous co-founder, CEO Dario Amodei . Databricks, Anduril and others Databricks and Anduril, meanwhile, both have founders serving as CEOs who have amassed billion-dollar-plus net worths during their tenures. Databricks co-founder and CEO Ali Ghodsi has a reported $7.6 billion net worth , with the company he leads valued at around $190 billion following an August financing. Anduril co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf , meanwhile, has an estimated $1.5 billion net worth as a result of his stake in the $61 billion valuation defense industry disruptor. Co-founder Palmer Luckey , who sold his virtual reality startup Oculus to Meta for $2 billion in 2014 before starting Anduril, has an estimated $5.9 billion net worth. Several other founders and CEOs of startups that raised some of this year’s largest rounds are billionaires too. This includes Wonder founder Marc Lore , Figure founder Brett Adcock , and Surge AI founder and CEO Edwin Chen , among others. Billionaire categories We can split the billionaires who founded this year’s most heavily funded startups into two broad subcategories. There are those who became billionaires through the startup that just raised capital. And there are those who were already billionaires through prior companies or investments. Ghodsi, Amodei and Brockman fit in the first group. In the second group, of course, we can put Musk and Bezos, as well as Altman and Luckey, who became a 21-year-old billionaire following the Oculus sale. Historically, neither billionaire type was a particularly common recipient of venture funding rounds. The term “unicorn” as a moniker for private companies valued at $1 billion or more only entered the lexicon in 2013, when this asset class became noticeably large. In prior decades, founders and CEOs mostly only hit billionaire status after their startups went public or sold in high-priced acquisitions. Updating the venture archetype But times change. And in tandem, our image of what a startup funding recipient looks like should evolve as well. True, quite a bit of capital still flows to the stereotypical venture recipients: first-time founders or serial entrepreneurs whose prior companies didn’t make them fabulously wealthy. But a majority of venture funding now does not go to these classic startup types. Instead, it goes to companies with valuations already high enough to warrant billionaire status for their stakeholders as well as ventures founded by men who are already billionaires. title: China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October

payload.text: Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek . The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion. The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding. Funding concentration Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital , Index Ventures and Lux Capital . DeepSeek ’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance , and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI . DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI , a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board . The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity. Other large rounds last month went to Axiom , which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp , which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent , which says it  raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its  headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi , which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes , which raised a $1 billion Series A. AI-driven A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI , which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev. A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month. Exits The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX ’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion . On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber ’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion. Looking ahead With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds. The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time. Data is as of Nov. 2, 2026. Cohere is targeting a $5 billion funding that was announced in October, without reporting an initial or final close . This funding was not included in the October monthly totals. Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year. Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price. Glossary of funding terms Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million. Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round. payload.text: Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3. Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups. Large rounds dominate funding One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more. As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023. The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic . But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds. Deals keep falling even as dollars rise In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared. In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year. The early-stage slump Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low. It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups , with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips. Looking ahead Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom. A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure. But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars. payload.text: Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question. Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech. The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count. AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning. The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019. Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.” Notable deals Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States. The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews , which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth , with participation from Atomico , HarbourVest Partners , Kinnevik , Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management . The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion. Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities , joined by New Alliance Capital , Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely , develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis. Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue. Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field , bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million. Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo , which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital , Isai and Ternel . The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments. Exits Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities. Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets , a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February. On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November. Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing. > **大模型时代的工程师分水岭：**  
> 别人还在写提示词问答，你已经能驾驭由 LLM 自主决策控制流的工业级 Agent 系统。

---

## 💡 为什么你需要这门课程？

2024~2026 年，大模型应用开发发生了一次关键心智跃迁：**从单一对话的 Chatbot ，走向拥有双手、记忆、规划与协作能力的 AI Agent （智能体）。**

但是，许多开发者在尝试把 Agent 搬上生产环境时，都会撞上同一堵墙：

- ❌ **难以控制**：模型调用外部工具频频格式出错、死循环；
- ❌ **状态失控**：多轮对话上下文越来越臃肿，记忆容易遗忘关键信息；
- ❌ **上线不敢用**：缺乏可观测追踪（ Tracing ），一旦报错无从排查，还面临 Prompt 注入攻击的风险。

把 Agent **从 Demo 变成工业级产品**，需要一套扎实严谨的**工程学科体系**。

为此，我们倾力打造了这套 **《 AI Agent 工程系统学习课程》** —— **28 节深度大课、11 大核心模块、覆盖 4 条定制化学习路径**，带你从底层 ReAct 推理循环，一路杀到企业级长任务工作流与加密审计！

---

## 🗺️ 课程全景知识图谱

本课程不堆砌概念，每一个章节都围绕**真实工程落地**展开：

![lx]( https://ai-agent-course-501.pages.dev/lessons/lx.jpg)

---

## 🎯 四条专属学习路径：按你的需求随到随学

28 节课体系完整，但你不必从头刷到尾。我们按工程师的典型场景，量身定制了四条高效学习路径：

| 学习路径                | 目标受众                            | 推荐学习课时                                           | 攻克目标                                                     |
| :---------------------- | :---------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- |
| **路径 A · 转岗求职**   | 想转型 AI 应用/Agent 架构岗的工程师 | **L0 → L1 → L2 → L3 → L4 → L5 → L6 → L7 → L8 → L9**    | 3-4 周搞定理清核心概念，手写 ReAct 循环，精通框架对比与架构图绘制 |
| **路径 B · 快速救火**   | 手头有正在落地的 Agent 业务项目     | **L1 → L2 → L4 → L14 → L15 → L19 → L21**               | 直击工具设计、上下文工程、记忆存储、线上可观测性，立即投入实战 |
| **路径 C · 走向生产**   | 平台架构师、负责高可用企业级系统    | **L5 → L11 → L14 → L15 → L16 → L19 → L20 → L22 → L23** | 掌握 MCP 协议、企业级 MAF 框架、Saga 补偿长事务、Ed25519 签名审计 |
| **路径 D · 安全与可靠** | 风控、安全审计与合规专家            | **L11 → L13 → L22 → L26 → L27**                        | 掌握 Prompt 直接/间接注入四层防护、威胁建模、CI/CD 自动化测试金字塔 |

---

## 🔗 立即开始学习

点击下方官方部署直达链接，直达核心实战课时，开启你的 AI Agent 架构师跃迁之旅：

👉 **课程访问入口**：  
[https://ai-agent-course-501.pages.dev]( https://ai-agent-course-501.pages.dev)

---

*(欢迎转发分享给正在做 LLM 与 Agent 落地开发的技术伙伴，共同搭建可信赖的智能体系统！)*

title: Zenith
summary: a developer platform for shipping and selling your app

extra.author: l-mdev
extra.original_title: Show HN: Zenith, a developer platform for shipping and selling your app

story_text.value:
Hi HN! I'm Liam and I'm one of the people building Zenith.

Most selfhosted apps ship with the best features switched off. OAuth, email and AI need users to provide accounts, API keys, an SMTP server that whoever runs the app (on their own servers!) don't have, so developers leave out the best features. And the people most willing to pay for an app usually can't run a server at all.

Zenith is a place to ship and sell those apps with the features on from day one. We simply extend Docker compose with an x-zenith: object to get a zenith-compose.yml, and inside the block you can set up OpenAI compatible API, SMTP, Sign in with Zenith, secret management, filebrowser, etc all autoconfigured though environment variables.

With the cli you can do a `zenith publish` and get a spot on the marketplace and a cut of the revenue. Your users can then deploy a fully managed instance. Want to test emails with SMTP? You can spin up an identical preview deployment with `zenith up` and it just works.

On the roadmap is Resend and Twillio compatible email, SMS APIs, Sign in with ChatGPT, Google account connections, GPUs, sitewide notifications (mobile app maybe?)

We'd love to know which integration you'd want next, and see what apps you publish! Supercharge your project today!

    npm install -g @zenith-hosting/cli

title.value: Show HN: Zenith, a developer platform for shipping and selling your app

title: Kids Shelf
summary: your kids' own little internet

extra.author: ericd
extra.original_title: Show HN: Kids Shelf, your kids' own little internet

story_text.value:
Hey all, I made this server for spinning up a local network page for our (young) kids to host videos and manage video watching time without turning them loose on main youtube, with all its random brainrot and engagement boosting optimizations (no autoplay next video here).

- MIT licensed, no tracking scripts anywhere, do whatever you want with it, I have no interest in commercializing this

- Gives them a daily "video minutes allowance", and enforces it for us (ours get 10 minutes each, they watch it together, and it rolls over, so some days they watch nothing, others they watch for an hour).

- Science/education videos can be set to half cost or free

- Includes yt-dlp baked in, the admin screen takes youtube URLs and downloads them locally

- Point it at other local/network video folders

- Hardware transcoding with ffmpeg baked in

- Also includes kiwix, which hosts wikipedia, all the project gutenberg kids literature, the minecraft wiki, etc etc

- Has a little math practice thing, if they set new speed records, it gives them more minutes

This was tailor made for us, and I just cleaned it up/open sourced it for public consumption, so there are probably still some rough edges. If you give it a try, and have any suggestions, please let me know! I'm new to open sourcing stuff, so any feedback on how to do that right welcome.

title: K8sman
summary: A Native Kubernetes IDE

extra.author: agenericname
extra.original_title: Show HN: K8sman – A Native Kubernetes IDE

story_text.value:
Hi HN, k8sman is a native lighter-weight Kubernetes IDE.

It’s a Flutter GUI on top of a Go backend that works with client-go and your existing kubeconfig. Nothing installed in the cluster and no telemetry whatsoever.

Just some of the features I think are unique:

- Low footprint (~ 50% RSS compared to Lens on the same cluster)

- Inspector panels for 30+ kinds that explain what's wrong (a crash-looping pod shows its exit code, termination message and a link to the previous instance's logs)

- Customisable views with a compact query language (status!=Running restarts>3 age<1h), with sortable, resizable and reorderable columns that persist per kind

- Streamed logs with searching, pod terminals, alerts, port-forwards that persist across pod restarts, and local shell with kubectl that follows the cluster you look at

- Helm history with diffs between revisions, rollbacks and dry-run upgrades

- Read-only mode per context (enabled by default for everything that looks like prod)

- Integrated with Argo CD, Prometheus, Trivy image scanning (but works just as well without!)

Builds for macOS, Windows and Linux. Apache 2.0.

title: Strive and Seek
summary: original merch for builders, hackers and founders

extra.author: byosko
extra.original_title: Show HN: Strive and Seek – original merch for builders, hackers and founders

story_text.value:
It all started with a poster in our office that says "Fck it, ship it".

People really gravitate to the poster. Take pictures with it. Tell us, "we love the sentiment!"

So we decided: why not launch a shop?

Strive & Seek is a side project with our own designs for builders, hackers, founders, etc.

Some designs are more upbeat. Others lean into the more realistic challenges of building things: "Born to Code, Forced to Fundraise" is an example.

We shouldn't pretend building stuff that works, creates value and scales is easy. We hope Strive & Seek provides a bit of encouragement, when necessary, or simply does a good job of accurately describing the week you're having.

It all started with a simple "Fck it, ship it" poster. Now we'll see if anyone else enjoys the designs, messages and sentiment as much as we do.

Appreciate any feedback!

title: Firenook
summary: Firebase emulators in Rust: 40× faster writes, 10× less RAM

extra.author: sanjevirau
extra.original_title: Show HN: Firenook – Firebase emulators in Rust: 40× faster writes, 10× less RAM

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we have been developing with Firebase for a long time, and the only way Firebase developers can build apps without directly costing them is using the official Firebase Emulator Suite.

However, the issue with this suite is, it's dependent and running on Java with a old Console UI (not updated in years), that was not built to support tons and millions of data and has pretty bad developer experience. For a long time, we were hitting Out of Memory on even high specs laptop while developing and the worst part is while this happens all the persists data keep getting lost.

We were honestly frustrated with this, and thought what if we built the Firebase Emulator Suite the right way, as it always should have been.

Introducing Firenook, a faster drop-in replacement for Firebase Emulator Suite for Firebase developers. It's 40x faster writes and needs 10x less RAM to run it. We took the right approach of first building it Rust as a single engine, so that there will be no Java dependencies and built from scratch a new Console UI using modern web stacks.

The result is, now we were able to run 2 millions datas loaded to Firenook with only taking around 2GB ram compared to 22GB of the official suite. Things are way faster and rebuilt Console UI gives best developer experience from logging Firebase Functions, to editing Firestore documents in JSON and many more.

We developed this throughly for around 2 months now and ran this internally for a month before we decided it's time to release it to public so that other devs can make use of Firenook and also contribute it to make it better.

Firenook is still new and I'm sure it misses things. So please try it our on your project and let us if there are any issues.

Thank you.

title.value: Show HN: Firenook – Firebase emulators in Rust: 40× faster writes, 10× less RAM

payload.author: sanjevirau
payload.story_text:
Hi HN, we have been developing with Firebase for a long time, and the only way Firebase developers can build apps without directly costing them is using the official Firebase Emulator Suite.

However, the issue with this suite is, it's dependent and running on Java with a old Console UI (not updated in years), that was not built to support tons and millions of data and has pretty bad developer experience. For a long time, we were hitting Out of Memory on even high specs laptop while developing and the worst part is while this happens all the persists data keep getting lost.

We were honestly frustrated with this, and thought what if we built the Firebase Emulator Suite the right way, as it always should have been.

Introducing Firenook, a faster drop-in replacement for Firebase Emulator Suite for Firebase developers. It's 40x faster writes and needs 10x less RAM to run it. We took the right approach of first building it Rust as a single engine, so that there will be no Java dependencies and built from scratch a new Console UI using modern web stacks.

The result is, now we were able to run 2 millions datas loaded to Firenook with only taking around 2GB ram compared to 22GB of the official suite. Things are way faster and rebuilt Console UI gives best developer experience from logging Firebase Functions, to editing Firestore documents in JSON and many more.

We developed this throughly for around 2 months now and ran this internally for a month before we decided it's time to release it to public so that other devs can make use of Firenook and also contribute it to make it better.

Firenook is still new and I'm sure it misses things. So please try it our on your project and let us if there are any issues.

Thank you.

title: Nico
summary: a two-agent type personal agent on your Mac

extra.author: benjushi
extra.original_title: Show HN: Nico – a two-agent type personal agent on your Mac

story_text.value:
Hi HN. I'm Brian, I make Xmind, the most popular mind mapping app, since 2006. This is my new project Nico, a personal agent for the Mac.

Every huge companies are building personal agents right now. The part I think matters most is the two-agent structure, so that's what Nico is built around.

The front agent talks to you. Always available, only one session, one memory, continuously compaction, and it carries almost no tools, so it can answer fast.

The worker agent does the job. It picks up tasks the front agent puts in an inbox and reports back when they're done. It almost never talks to you; anything it needs goes through the front agent.

I think this is the real step forward, but the attention goes to the cloud computer. I get why: you can hand the agent a task from your phone. But, it also makes everything more complicated. People need to upload the entire environment while

So I built one with the cloud computer taken out. Nico is a native Mac app. You hold the right ⌘ key (or fn) and talk; the front agent answers by voice; the worker agent is pi (github.com/earendil-works/pi) runs by your own AI subscription, in a sandbox.

With computer-use (via cua-driver), browser-use (via a browser extension), and a built-in browser, she can clean up your desktop, or answer "why is my Mac so hot". If you say "this", she looks at the screenshot of the active window. Most tasks run without you; sending an email waits for your click.

The downside: when you're not at your Mac, you can't use it. I haven't figured out what to do about that.

Would you want a personal agent that only lives on your Mac?

Chronosphere rebuilds a PR in logical steps to try to recreate the train of thought that went into the generation of the PR itself. title: Aggregate Finance
summary: your financial data in a spreadsheet you own

extra.author: mitchthebaker
extra.original_title: Show HN: Aggregate Finance, your financial data in a spreadsheet you own

story_text.value:
I started building Aggregate Finance a couple of years ago because I was manually updating a Google Sheet to track my credit card statements, monthly recurring transactions, and spending habits. This seemed perfect for automation as I was having to log in to six separate banking apps to pull this information together.

My original intention was to use this tool locally, but I figured it would be an excellent learning opportunity to understand how to scale the application for others to use. The core functionality of Aggregate Finance revolves around syncing banks and brokerages through Plaid to create visuals and data analytics in Google Sheets and OneDrive/Excel, but I've also added Stripe for payments, passkey and TOTP support for MFA (wanted to better learn how WebAuthn works, mostly), and Resend for emailing account updates.

The first question you're likely thinking is: isn't this just reinventing the wheel? There's plenty of other personal finance/budgeting apps out there like Rocket Money, Monarch, Copilot Money, YNAB, Tiller, Credit Karma, etc. I personally tried Rocket Money but it left a bad taste in my mouth how my entire financial history was stored on their servers without having direct ownership of the data. Another pain point with these personal finance apps is you're locked into their subscription and lose access to your financial data if you cancel.

That's why I opted for the Google Sheet and OneDrive/Excel approach since this persists financial data over time and provides direct data ownership. There's a fair argument that these options still share your financial data with Google or Microsoft, so I built a way to download your financial data locally via CSV/Excel/LibreOffice exports.

In terms of data encryption, Aggregate Finance encrypts financial data before it reaches MongoDB: balances, transactions, merchants, statements, holdings, and any user customizations. Each user gets their own AES-256 key rather than a shared key. The reason I went with this approach is for data deletion: when someone deletes their account, their encryption key is deleted as well, so any financial data stored in prior database backups can't be decrypted.

I've been using Aggregate Finance with my own live bank accounts and investment holdings, and it's already been helpful. I can see when my credit card statements are due, monitor my entire investment portfolio, keep track of recurring charges, create budgets, and see how my spending pans out over a given month or over the past year. I'm curious whether it's useful for anyone else, and I'd of course welcome any feedback on how I can improve it. You can try it with a free sample spreadsheet that contains a year of example data with no bank connection required at https://app.aggregatefi.com.

title: Gauge
summary: Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs

extra.author: 0x63_Problems
extra.original_title: Show HN: Gauge – Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Evan from Gauge. We’re open-sourcing our CLI to recursively improve your docs for coding agents. The CLI includes a local execution backend, so you don't need an account to try it. Explainer video here: https://youtu.be/zhLUlIKB1Mg

The CLI supports a hillclimbing loop:

- set up tasks for coding agents that would need your docs, like 'set up Gauge CI checks'

- run the tasks

- analyze session transcripts for friction or failures

- create variants of your docs to resolve the issues

- re-run the tasks with the doc variants injected (transparently, at the same hostname)

- repeat until you have a variant that resolves the issues

The same loop supports hillclimbing your Skills, CLI, and other agent-facing surfaces.

We started out 2 years ago building open-source developer tools (like Tach https://github.com/tach-org/tach), then pivoted to AI Search optimization, and are now focused on the intersection of the two spaces. We were already working with awesome devtool companies, and they were the first ones to ask us how to optimize for Claude Code and Codex. We realized this would be something that eventually every company needs to do. Our CLI provides primitives for docs/devrel/eng teams to measure, analyze, and improve how coding agents use their product.

The design boils down to two components: VMs and a network gateway.

The VMs are straightforward, we want the agents to be highly privileged within their environment so that they are representative of developers' coding agents. Each VM generally comes with the agent harness itself, language toolchains, and a git repository.

The network gateway is where we terminate TLS and swap in variants of your docs transparently. The gateway also handles credential replacement, so agents see placeholders and can't exfiltrate keys.

The CLI comes with a 'local' execution backend (inference is still remote). For VMs, it uses Docker containers, and the network gateway is mitmproxy running in a sidecar container for each session.

We've used the hillclimbing loop internally to find and fix coding agent issues like mistaken pricing, inaccurate product limitations, and repeated workarounds. We saw coding agents report that Gauge only supports Claude Code and Codex, traced it back to the web pages they fetched, and fixed the behavior (we support Pi, OpenCode, and Antigravity as well). For Clerk, we helped shift coding agents from their legacy 'keyless' mode to their new 'clerk init' command. They were able to validate a pre-release change to their SDK's error messages using Gauge, then saw a 3x increase in coding agents using 'clerk init' post-deploy.

Due to the 'static' nature of AI models, we've realized that closed-loop optimization techniques are now possible for essentially all software products. The same agent can be simulated over and over, meaning that a high-fidelity testing environment is all you need. Achieving the best results boils down to high-quality analysis (finding generalizable friction and objections) and paired experiments (vary only the content, measure the downstream change in behavior).

The repo is here: https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli and you can start using the CLI with: npm i -g @withgauge/cli

We also have documentation and a quickstart here: https://docs.withgauge.com/agents/guides/cli

If you point a coding agent at those pages, it should guide you through the initial setup - let us know if it doesn't! The intention is for your agent to run some sensible evaluations and find at least one point of friction you can fix.

We'd love to know from HN: Has anyone tried to DIY this locally, or built something in-house at their company? Is this an improvement? If not, what would need to change?

summary: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)

extra.author: schopra909
extra.original_title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)

story_text.value:
My brother and I run a 2-person lab that trains our own generative video models from scratch. The ultimate goal is a set of creative tools that make it easier for anyone to make animation.

Video models today are too slow/expensive and lack sufficient controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. In our opinion, they're not usable yet for storytelling.

When we set out to build Linum v3 (our next video model) earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools.

Typically, you see "latent diffusion models". A VAE (Variational Autoencoder) compresses the input data into a smaller "latent space" and the diffusion model learns how to generate within this subspace.

Over the past few months, we've been publishing our work on efficient pixel-space diffusion models. These throw away the VAE, having the diffusion model learn a latent-space optimized for its exact task.

This serves 3 purposes: 1) Simplify Architecture (no 2-stage model training) 2) Faster Convergence (11x faster convergence vs. our latent diffusion counterpart) 3) Cheaper Inference (4x more aggressive token reduction in attention context-windows, without significant loss in quality)

This past month we were pressure testing our latest architecture (Pyramid-JiT) by training a text-to-image model longer than the typical one-off experiment. Specifically, we trained it for ~$20K on 660M samples.

We were surprised by the quality of results, so we thought we'd release it as open weights for the community (Apache 2.0). The research itself is already public, on our website.

For us, it's a big stepping stone towards cheaper video models, since pretty much all video models start as image models. We like to say these models have to learn nouns before they learn verbs.

title: scrollhope
summary: I built a Bible verse feed to replace doomscrolling

extra.author: jclardy
extra.original_title: Show HN: I built a Bible verse feed to replace doomscrolling

story_text.value:
Hey all, I just released my latest iOS app, Scroll Hope. It is a tiktok like scrolling feed, but the content is Bible verses with fun dynamic backgrounds. It also tracks your reading progress and keeps stats over time.

You can try it out on the website, or on iOS if you want the app lockout feature which lets you block your social apps. Completely free, with the option to support the app with a tip and unlock some additional icon and sharing options.

Coming soon is audio and auto-scroll, so you can set the phone down and read/listen hands free.

Android is on the way, the lockout feature is taking some additional review time.

title: AI Gude
summary: my feeds as a daily podcast, revived with AI

extra.author: alex0ptr
extra.original_title: Show HN: AI Gude – my feeds as a daily podcast, revived with AI

story_text.value:
Hi HN. AI Gude turns the news you follow into a short morning podcast, written and read by AI. It is open source and you host it yourself. “Ei Gude” is Hessian for good morning.

Some background: I started this about a year and a half ago and never got back to it, because I became a father and my free time was gone. AI is what changed that. It was the game changer that finally unleashed the project. I listen to my own episodes every day now, so it is useful to me. I’m still at the very beginning, though.

What I would love: ideas and feedback, and recommendations for good TTS models. I use Gemini’s TTS today and want to know what else is worth trying for ten-minute episodes, ideally good in German and English, hosted or self-hostable. What do you use?

title: Rivet (YC W23)
summary: Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3

extra.author: NathanFlurry
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3

story_text.value:
Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet (https://rivet.dev) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3.

Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle.

It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable.

Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c

When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. This led us to extend our game server orchestrator to support what we call Rivet Actors today: many lightweight workers with in-memory state and durable storage. By using actors, we were able to serve tens of millions of monthly active users.

As agents grew in popularity, it became clear that running agents in sandboxes is inefficient. Sandboxes are expensive, mostly idle, and slow to start. Developers started using actors because they are far more memory efficient (72 KB baseline for actors vs 512 MB for a minimal sandbox) and fast to start (4.9 ms p99 for actors vs 1.7 s p99 for sandboxes).

For example, Amp is using Rivet to orchestrate multiplayer agents. They originally tried to build on Cloudflare Durable Objects, but couldn’t launch because of the platform’s limitations and unresponsive support. They migrated to Rivet Actors in a weekend and deploy on-prem. Rivet’s flexible architecture lets them adapt it to their own use cases without being constrained by a framework or the memory, storage, and runtime limits of Cloudflare Durable Objects.

Under the hood, Rivet is backed by S3 while maintaining SSD speeds.

Why S3? Previously, Rivet ran on FoundationDB. However, we were surprised to find that companies are storing orders of magnitude more data on Rivet Actors than in Postgres, such as large session transcripts, agent artifacts, and full POSIX filesystems. As their data grew, they had to start paying for SSDs that sat mostly idle with old transcripts. This led us to double down on S3 as our primary storage medium without sacrificing performance. This choice means that data stored on Rivet is 10× cheaper than on EBS gp3 while maintaining SSD speeds.

It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost:

When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors.

This architecture lets Rivet provide 1.07 ms durable writes (3 AZ, p99), 1.36 ms reads (p99), and 138 ms reads from object storage (p99).

We’ve spent a lot of time making sure that Rivet can run wherever you need it. Self-hosting requires deploying a single Rust binary with S3 as the only dependency, Rivet Cloud lets you deploy dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region, and BYOC lets us deploy Rivet to your VPC without having to operate it yourself. Rivet also runs identically in local dev as in production, since Rivet is a lightweight binary that runs anywhere

Rivet Actors can be written in TypeScript or Rust. Out of the box, they support agents (Pi Durable), workflows, real-time, multiplayer, running AI-generated code, Durable Streams, and integrations with tools like Vercel’s Eve and Turso. See all of our available guides, or point your agent at them: https://rivet.dev/docs/#guides

Try it out now, by reading our quickstart guides (https://rivet.dev/docs/) or ask your agent: “Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then build a multiplayer chat agent and run it locally.”

We’d love to get feedback on your experience with Rivet! We’re deeply invested in making Rivet an easy-to-self-host, flexible, and efficient way to run agentic workloads.

GitHub: https://github.com/rivet-dev/rivet

Architecture: https://rivet.dev/docs/architecture/

Benchmarks: https://rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking/

Self-hosting: https://rivet.dev/docs/deploy/self-host/

title: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
summary: AI media manager and video editor

extra.author: lukeigel
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor

story_text.value:
Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino (https://kino.ai). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at https://kino.ai/launch-video

Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack.

Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match.

Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way.

To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny.

I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America (https://regressions.net). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet.

Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing.

Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing.

We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning up agents to make new videos every day, then using review links to flag issues. One founder ships ads like this: each day he uses Kino's YouTube support to find b-roll he is allowed to use, he edits something, his co-founder leaves notes such as “we need to use this clip instead” and his agent can then apply them. Full-time filmmakers are also using Kino. They tend to resemble “toxenmaxxer” software developers, where 15+ agents iterate on a single project, each trusting Kino as the source of truth for timeline state, graphics, media, everything.

The full editor is free, including unlimited imports and exports, real-time collaboration and MCP access for your own agent. Pro is $25 per editor per month and adds unlimited MCP tool calls, share links, more storage, YouTube search, and the ability to edit alongside your team. You can download it at https://kino.ai. We have not yet released Kino for the pure web browser, just Electron for now.

If you make videos personally, if you have ProRes media and you want to try to break Kino, if you have legacy video editor projects to bring in, or if you want to make more content for your company, we'd love to hear how Kino works for you.

title: Ask HN
summary: What's your current AI agentic setup?

extra.author: eggbrain
extra.original_title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?

story_text.value:
I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI.

1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc)

- Which tiers?

- Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)?

2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models.

- Which models and providers?

3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses?

- What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)?

4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools?

- For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom.

5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse?

- If you are using them, what are your main use cases?

-----

I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.

title: ollama/ollama: v0.40.15
summary:
## MiMo V2.6

Xiaomi MiMo's [mimo-v2.6](https://ollama.com/library/mimo-v2.6), a 9B model built for code and agent workflows, is now supported in Ollama.

```sh
ollama run mimo-v2.6
```

## AutoTrust decision models

[AutoTrust](https://ollama.com/library/autotrust-jev) decision models read text and return choices, yes or no probabilities, and ratings for the questions you supply. The family includes 9b, 35b, and 27b-vl sizes — the 35b and 27b-vl sizes can also read images.

```sh
ollama run autotrust-jev "A customer says their card was charged twice." --ask "Is this a billing issue?"
```

Note: autotrust-jev is supported on Apple silicon in this release.

## What's Changed

 - ollama launch now supports Kimi Code CLI — the successor to kimi-cli — and offers to migrate existing kimi-cli setups
 - ollama launch now fills in Pi's model list automatically so models can be picked inside Pi, and Claude Desktop's model
   picker shows Ollama's actual model names
 - Recurrent and vision GGUF models can now serve more than one request at a time
 - Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models using long-context (YaRN) scaling
 - Running ollama with no arguments opens the welcome launcher

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/compare/v0.40.14...v0.40.15
