title: 国行版苹果 AI 开始测试；ChatGPT 搜索量已达到谷歌 20%；Seedance 被曝五成收入来自海外｜极客早知道
summary: 国行 Apple 智能开始测试：iOS 27.3 首个开发者 Beta 版已推送 11 月 4 日，苹果向开发者推送 iOS 27.3 首个 Beta 版，国行 iPhone 用户开始测试首批 Apple 智能功能，包括实时翻译、照片消除、写作工具和通知摘要等。国行 Apple 智能与阿里巴巴达成合作，在部分体验中接入千问。国内用户可直接在 Siri、写作工具和视觉智能中调用千问，覆盖文本与图像理解相关能力。 这次开放的是开发者测试版，正式版计划于 12 月推出。首批支持 iPhone 15 Pro 系列、iPhone 16 及后续机型，以及 iPhone Air 和 iPhone Duo；WWDC 2026 发布的新版 Siri AI 暂未包含在内。（来源：快科技） 腾讯 12.8 亿用户蝉联中国互联网第一，绿泡泡月活破 1.5 亿，手游 top10 独占 8 款 11 月 3 日，QuestMobile 发布最新《中国移动互联网秋季大报告》。报告显示，截至 2026 年 9 月，腾讯控股以 12.80 亿去重总用户量（APP + 小程序）位列中国互联网公司用户规模榜首，第九年蝉联榜首，霸主地位稳固。 短剧业务是本次报告的关注重点。腾讯旗下嵌入微信生态的绿泡泡短剧 2026 年 9 月月活跃用户规模达到 1.56 亿，登顶微信小程序短剧月活榜。该产品依托微信社交关系链与视频号导流快速起量，目前体量已是短剧行业第二名，增长速度很快。 游戏业务方面，2026 年 9 月手机游戏 App 月活跃用户 TOP10 中，腾讯独占 8 款，合计月活约 3.41 亿。其中，王者荣耀以 1.29 亿月活位居全行业第二，仅次于乐元素开心消消乐的 1.61 亿；三角洲行动、和平精英分别以 6675 万、3547 万月活位列第三、第四。报告同时提到，名古屋亚运会期间，王者荣耀以庞大玩家基数成为电竞项目顶流。 报告指出，短剧视频与短视频已成为驱动全网用户时长增长的核心引擎，增长贡献率达 111.5%。依托微信社交与私域流量，小程序短剧起量迅猛，短剧业务正成为腾讯盘活流量矩阵的重要抓手。（来源：雷锋网） OpenAI 将停用旧版 ChatGPT Classic 应用，合并聊天和工作标签页 11 月 3 日，据科技网站 9to5mac 报道，OpenAI 已通知仍在使用旧版 ChatGPT Classic 应用的用户，该应用将很快停用。同时，OpenAI 也正在准备将聊天 (Chat) 和工作 (Work) 合并为一个统一的界面。 尽管此前种种迹象已经表明，旧版应用即将走向停用，但如今官方终于给出了具体日期。根据用户打开 ChatGPT Classic 时看到的新提示信息，该应用将于 2027 年 1 月 30 日正式停止提供服务。 「这款应用将于 2027 年 1 月 30 日正式停止服务。请使用新版 ChatGPT 应用，体验最新功能。你的全部聊天记录都会迁移过去，你可以继续之前未完成的对话。」OpenAI 称。 OpenAI 正在告知用户，未来几周内将开始测试整合 Chat 和 Work 功能的统一体验。几个月前，OpenAI 总裁格雷格·布罗克曼 (Greg Brockman) 曾承认，新版 ChatGPT 界面「确实有点混乱」。他当时表示，公司希望在年底前取消 Work 标签页，将其功能整合到常规 ChatGPT 体验中。（来源：cnBeta） 苹果开放 Siri AI 第三方 App 操作能力，开发者可让 AI 执行复杂任务 11 月 4 日，苹果开始向开发者推送 iOS 27.3 Developer Preview，进一步开放 Siri AI 对第三方 App 的操作能力。新版本允许开发者向 Siri 提供应用内操作接口。 Siri 可以结合自然语言指令、个人上下文和屏幕内容执行任务，而不仅是打开某个 App。苹果还引入「App Skills」机制，让开发者把多个操作组合成一个可调用的任务。例如，用户通过网约车 App 叫车后，可以直接让 Siri 修改上车地点，而不必重新进入 App 完成全部操作。这次更新也扩展了 Siri 对苹果自有应用的操作能力，覆盖日历、文件、邮件、地图、照片和 Safari 等产品。（来源：The Verge） 苹果调整 App 年龄分级：约会及恋爱类功能最低 18+ 11 月 3 日，苹果发布公告，宣布自 11 月 16 日起，在 App Store

title: 拿下近亿美元融资后，他们造了个开放动态真实世界的「行动伙伴」
summary: 作者｜苏子华 编辑｜郑玄 博尔赫斯 写过一则著名的寓言。一个帝国的制图师们绘制了一张与领土等大的地图，精确到每一寸土地、每一条河流。后代人发现这张地图毫无用处，把它弃置在荒野中，任其腐烂。 真正在一个地方走路的人，靠的从来不是一张一比一的图纸，而是脚底的感觉、眼睛的判断，以及走错了再调整的能力。 具身智能行业正在上演这则寓言的现实版。 过去两年，人形机器人学会了跳舞、翻跟头、弹钢琴。但一个略显尴尬的事实是，这些编排的动作，大多是提前反复排练，且发生在受控的封闭环境里。如果放在现实社会的开放环境中，这些机器人该怎么办，它们到底能帮你干什么？ 费莫一科技 （PHYMI）试图回答这个命题。成立初期便完成近亿美元种子轮融资，由 IDG 资本领投，云启资本、滴滴出行、复星锐正、耀途资本、禾赛科技跟投。融资消息仅公布一个月后，它便推出首款行动伙伴。 行动伙伴 Sagi｜图片来源：PHYMI 10 月 28 日，Sagi（萨其玛）正式发布，是行业内首个定位「行动伙伴」的 Physical Agent。Sagi 采用 四轮足 、人形上身、背着小型货箱的机器人，英文名取自人马座。辨识度鲜明的身体，它没有追求像人，围绕长程移动、操作与承载共同设计；「行动伙伴」则定义了它与人的关系：理解人的目标，能够独立担当，也能够相互协作。 但它具备极其实用、且当下行业里极为罕见的能力：接收一个目标，然后在一个开放、动态、真实的场景里，将跨场景移动与物品操作连接起来，遇到需要判断或帮助的情况，再通过 LINK 与人协作，持续推进任务，完成全流程交付。 费莫一创始人 刘念邱 ，此前是元戎启行的技术合伙人、董事，亲历高阶自动驾驶从 L4 研发运营走向规模化量产的关键阶段，参与无图智驾方案落地，以及技术体系向端到端模型、 VLA 大模型演进。再往前，他是英特尔的高级工程师，做过智能硬件的连续创业者。 在具身智能赛道愈发拥挤的 2026 年，PHYMI 没有追求酷炫 demo，而是选了一条看似朴实、实则困难得多的路。在刘念邱看来，「开放场景才是真正的考场。」 为什么是「行动伙伴」？ 费莫一的第一款产品，绕开了行业里最普遍的叙事。 刘念邱告诉极客公园，更希望用「伙伴」来定义他们推出的 Physical Agent，「因为我们首先关心的是，用户希望它帮助自己完成什么，以及它能够创造什么价值。」 在他看来，Physical Agent 的核心是，站在用户的立场，理解他的想法、拆解他的目标，通过长程移动、操作和交互，在物理世界中把事情做成。「即使人不在现场，也可以把目标交给它，让它独立推进；遇到信息不足或需要判断的情况，人也能通过 LINK 提供帮助，共同完成任务。」 「行动伙伴」干的，不是人做不了的事，而是人不想干的事——承接的是人需要亲自到场、跨越不同地点并连续执行的事务，拓展人的行动能力。这种定位差异背后，本质是一场关于「人与机器关系」的重新倒置。 传统服务机器人的逻辑，本质上是改造环境以适应机器人：要进写字楼，先得铺设专用的磁条引导线、贴满 QR 码定位标签、打通电梯系统的无线协议，甚至提前用激光雷达将几千平米的物理空间毫厘不差地建图。人类世界必须为了机器人做出改造。 而费莫一的思路恰恰相反—— 应该让 Physical Agent 适应人类生活的社会，而不是让人类社会一直去适应它。 真实世界天然是开放的、动态的、乱糟糟且充满意外的。前台的箱子可能被临时挪动，走廊里随时有行人穿过，办公室的门可能是半掩着的。「人的生活和工作天然发生在不同地点，一个目标往往包含多个相互关联的步骤。任务执行过程中，环境、物品和人的需求还会变化。」 刘念邱表示，Sagi 的设计初心，就是直接丢进这种未经改造的真实环境里。Sagi 没有一上来就挑战人类手部极限的精细活，比如拧螺丝、缝合伤口、弹钢琴等等，而是优先建设开放动态场景中的长程移动与操作能力。取放、携带和交付，是验证这些能力的具体任务；关键在于机器人如何将多个地点、动作与反馈连接成完整过程。 看似不够科幻，但实际上这是在 Day 1 就选择了一条极难、直接挑战「深水区」的路线：开放动态场景中的长程移动与操作。 可以说，开放场景才是真正的考场——空间无法提前穷举，物品和人的需求随时变化，机器人必须基于实时感知理解环境、围绕用户目标自主行动，而不是在排练好的舞台上表演。 刘念邱解释说，长程移动是费莫一的一项差异化能力。「机器人要能够自己到达用户需要它出现的地方，才能接触更丰富的场景、承担更多工作。同时，移动与操作缺一不可：到达之后需要与物品交互，跨场景行动中的开门、乘梯等环节，也可能需要两者协同。」 这种「长程」，不仅是物理空间上的数百米跨越，更是任务持续时间、步骤数量以及面对突发状况时连续决策的跨度。 这正是「行动伙伴」所代表的技术含金量。 开箱即用： 不建图、不改场地，拉过来就干活 在费莫一展示的真实场景 Demo 中，Sagi 展现出了极强的自如感。 在社区快递站，它穿梭于堆满纸箱的狭窄通道间，识别出目标包裹后，由上身双臂抱起放入背箱，随后自主搭乘电梯送达住户门前： 在办公园区，它接到指令后可以穿越大堂、电梯、楼宇，帮忙递送物品： 而在公园露营场景中，面对崎岖不平的草地和随机摆放的折叠椅，它依然能够平稳行驶，驮着物资跟在人身边，随时接下临时的新需求： 这些场景之所以能够流畅运行，关键在于费莫一祭出的杀手锏——开箱即用，免部署。 对于传统服务机器人来说，进场前的建图、调试、改环境往往要折腾一整周时间。据介绍，在当前支持的环境和任务范围内，Sagi 第一次进入陌生环境，不需要工程人员先来「扫描打点」。启动之后，它会直接在执行任务的过程中边走边探索、寻找路径，并逐步形成记忆——就像一个新到岗的实习生，第一次去茶水间可能会看两眼路标，但走过一次后就自然记住了路线。 这份「无图运行」的底气，源于团队血脉里的技术基因。 作为元戎启行前技术合伙人，刘念邱是国内最早实现「无图智驾」攻坚的开拓者。团队在自动驾驶领域积累的经验，为这条路线提供了基础。可以迁移到具身智能领域的，包括降低先验依赖、基于实时感知理解环境、通过数据闭环持续迭代的方法，以及复杂软硬件协同和工程部署经验。 自动驾驶的「无图」解决的是车在马路上怎么开，而具身智能的「无图」面对的则是更复杂的三维物理世界。本质上，它们指向同一个底层哲学：让 AI 像人一样凭实时感知去适应陌生环境，而不是靠预先把世界全画下来。 为了支撑起这种开放环境下的长程能力，费莫一搭建了一套完整的四层技术支柱架构：大脑（BRAIN）+ 身体（BODY）+ 数据（DATA）+ 链接（LINK）。 我们来拆解一下这套结构的分工和背后的思考： 1.大脑：认知、行为、接触 不同于行业普遍采用的单一端到端大模型或简单级联方案，Sagi 搭载的 PHYMI BRAIN 1.0 采用了「异步分频多模态架构」，将机器人的思考与反应划分为三个空间： 认知空间： 负责「大局观」。理解人类意图，拆解长程任务，保持任务上下文，在面对突发阻碍时重新规划路线。 行为空间： 负责「眼手腿协同」。结合现场实时观测与物理预测，评估并生成下一步的具体动作策略。 接触空间： 负责「拿捏分寸」。以极高的频率处理力触觉反馈，确保在开门、拿取易碎物品时能够实时修正力道，实现安全的柔顺交互。 2.身体：实用主义的人马构型 在机器人的躯体形态上，费莫一率先采用了「四轮足 + 人形上身 + 随行背箱」的人马形态。 为什么是这种形态？ 刘念邱向极客公园解释道，腿部服务于通过性。四足提供稳定和承载基础，轮式移动兼顾长程行进效率。人形上身和双臂，则希望与人的操作方式对齐，适应人日常放置物品、开展工作的环境。背箱承担随行载物需求，减少运输过程中持续占用双臂的需要。 「背箱本质上是一种任务容器，可以根据不同需求调整配置。」刘念邱说。 他透露，团队并没有放弃双足。「双足体积更小，有机会进入更多空间；四轮足在稳定、承载等方面也有自身价值。我们认为多种形态会长期并存，人马形态本身也有长期需求。」 在产品边界上，他们不追求「万能」，而是先在一个场景里把一件事做到真正可用。 「现阶段希望先把第一个真实场景服务好，验证长程移动与操作的协同，再通过持续使用、数据反馈和模型迭代，逐步拓展任务与场景覆盖。」刘念邱说。 3.数据：经验如何变成能力 要让大脑学会在真实世界里干活，数据是核心。但现有的开源数据集大多局限于桌面前的近距离抓取。「一些现成采集方案更侧重近距离操作，未必能同时满足我们对远处细节和完整任务信息的需求，所以我们根据自己的任务要求，自研了采集设备。」刘念邱说。 费莫一自研的这套 360° 采集头环，结合了广角与长焦镜头，能够同步记录人类在复杂移动操作过程中的周边全局与细节视角。 真实场景采集、数据对齐与筛选、模型训练与评估、更新验证，再回到任务执行到反馈回流，一条高效的进化飞轮被彻底打通。 4.链接：人机协作的 「 伙伴 」 哲学 PHYMI LINK 是连接人与 Physical Agent 的实时交互系统，也是区域服务的调度中心。用户通过它交付目标、提供授权、了解进展，并在必要时补充信息或调整任务；区域内多个用户提出需求时，LINK 可以统筹调度多台机器人。在所有技术模块中，LINK 可能是最能体现「伙伴」一词含义的部分。 可以通过手机语音下达新的指令或沟通｜图片来源：PHYMI 刘念邱举了一个例子：你让 Sagi 去买可乐，它到了现场发现没有可乐，就可以通过 LINK 请求帮助。你通过 LINK 看到它当前看到的画面，查看其他饮料，确认换成哪一种并完成付款，它再根据更新后的需求继续执行。 「机器人帮人承担行动，人也在必要时帮助机器人推进任务。」刘念邱说，「我们希望这种协作让用户持续感受到价值，也让 Physical Agent 在真实使用中积累经验、提升能力。」 这种双向协作还体现在任务调度上。用户可以临时追加任务，系统会结合当前进度、任务约束与能力范围，调整后续计划。当区域内有多个用户提出需求时，LINK 可以统筹调度多台机器人，让已经开始的任务能够完成，新的需求也得到响应。 「不同用户的需求需要有执行顺序。机器人已经承接一个人的任务，其他人的新需求不能随意打断它。」刘念邱说，「新的需求进入 LINK 后，由调度中心统筹安排，可以调度区域内其他机器人承接，也可以安排后续执行。」 这个例子看似简单，但也道出了一个重要的产品哲学：机器人不是孤立的工具，而是嵌入在一个人机协作网络中的节点。它既需要自主性，也需要在关键时刻接受人的帮助和判断。 因此，也不难理解费莫一的产品节奏：先让机器人「到达」，再谈「操作」——长程移动与操作协同：机器人需要自己到达现场、完成交互，再根据反馈继续行动，才能承接更多真实任务，用得越多、数据越多，能力再一点点长。 Physical Agent： 从「伙伴」开始，重新定义落地的节奏 费莫一选择在 2026 年下场，是一个有意思的时间点。 刘念邱曾在访谈中表示，2024 年前后那波机器人创业潮，时机还没到——机器人专用关节电机、减速机供应链不成熟，AI 范式未收敛，数据闭环也没跑通。他判断，产品持续进化的核心，是它的「大脑」能力。 到 2026 年，他判断的三个条件同时到位：本体供应链成熟了，AI 基础设施充裕了，智驾行业也完整跑通了大规模数据闭环。 这个时间点，恰好也是整个行业的分水岭。 2026 年上半年，中国人形机器人出货量已超过 4 万台，全球占比 97%，市场规模迅速扩张；而另一面，演出租赁市场的泡沫正在出清，行业对于「能落地干活」的诉求变得迫切。 用户并不关心你的神经网络拥有多少亿参数，也不关心你的算法用了多么复杂的控制理论；用户只关心，下楼拿快递这件事，今天它到底能不能帮我跑一趟。 Sagi 的出现，正是呼应了当下行业的焦虑。机器人不一定非要只走弹钢琴、绣花等路线，它也可以只是一个帮你完成日常琐碎小事的行动伙伴。 这或许就是 Physical Agent 最触动人心的地方。它没有试图去用高不可攀的技术姿态去震撼人类，而是将最先进的技术，隐匿于一个个微小的生活场景之中。 虽然人工智能的技术巨浪席卷全球，但当下，我们很难要求每一个 Agent 都拥有超人般的头脑与躯干。能有这样一个默默无闻、开箱即用、随时准备帮你干活的「行动伙伴」，其实已经足够好。

title: 心言巴布「Bubbo 1」：一台机器人，如何成为家人
summary: 头图来源：心言机器人 2026 年 10 月 29 日，心言机器人正式发布具身家庭智能体「巴布（Bubbo 1）」。 这台毛绒外形的机器人，基于心言自研的 Bubbo OS，主打「伙伴式交互」：它不是一台等人发号施令的家电，而是一个会主动走近、主动回应的家庭成员。产品即日起在京东等官方渠道发售，售价 9499 元，前 1000 名订购者可享 7999 元。 在心言机器人创始人、Bubbo 1 首席设计师任永亮看来， 「 技术决定体验的下限，交互决定体验的上限。 」 过去的 AI，是你不开口它就不在的工具；而巴布要做的，是从「外部」视角搭起一个 Family Agent—— 识别家里的每一个人，也关注他们之间的关系。 为此，它在身上装了 13 类、26 个传感器，用 6 个自由度和两块表情屏理解复杂情感，再靠记忆、多模态感知和分级对话，给出有「延迟感、呼吸感、边界感」的回应。 发布环节结束后，任永亮与主持人、极客公园创始人张鹏，全国政协常委、国家统计局原副局长贾楠，哈尔滨工业大学计算学部长聘教授、博士生导师赵妍妍围坐在一起，讨论了一个问题：当机器人真正走进一个家庭，它该如何理解人、陪伴人，并长期留下来。 这是一场围绕「家人」展开的讨论。 在情感计算学者赵妍妍看来，机器人要跨越感知、认知、交互三层阶梯，才能从「看出你不开心」，走到「知道你为什么不开心」，进而给出有实质意义的帮扶。贾楠则用一组数据指出了产品背后的现实：截至 2025 年底，中国 60 岁以上人口已占常住人口的 23%，失能、独居老人将近 4000 万，而绝大多数老人仍希望居家养老。 任永亮把巴布定位为「家庭智能体」和伙伴，而不是工具或玩具。他最看重的功能，不是某项聪明的对话，而是「自动回充」——在他眼里，机器人要像一个物种那样，先学会在家庭环境中生存下去，「永不关机」。而衡量产品成功的标准，是它有一天学会了人类没有教过它的事。 「这是万里长征的第一步。」任永亮说。 以下为圆桌讨论实录，由极客公园整理： 一个「家人」的交卷时刻 张鹏： 永亮，记得两年前我还问你确认要上这艘船吗—— 从科技角度，这是件很难的事；但听完你的初心，我觉得它在人文上特别值得做，今天真心为你高兴。 接下来请两位朋友一起聊：全国政协常委、国家统计局原副局长贾楠，哈尔滨工业大学计算学部长聘教授、博士生导师赵妍妍。 两位看到巴布的功能和整个发布过程，印象最深刻的是什么？ 贾楠： 这已经是我第二次见到巴布了。今年 3 月两会之前，我第一次见到它，当时就眼前一亮——一个非常可爱的玩偶也好什么也好，就缓缓地走了进来，给我的第一感觉就是非常可爱。 刚才又听任总把整个创作、研制的过程做了详细介绍，我更有感触。当时我对巴布已经有所了解，主要是三大功能，其中对老人的陪伴这一块，是我们更加需要的。 非常感谢任总历经将近 10 年，投入了大量研发经费和精力。做这样的产品，前期必须有大量投入。在我们已经进入老龄化社会的情况下，现在具身机器人已经看得很多了，但像这样的陪伴式机器人，确实还很少。 张鹏： 对，在家庭场景里，明确想解决家庭情感和陪伴问题的，它是第一个。 贾楠： 它就像一个家庭里的小伙伴，家庭的一个成员。我觉得在当今社会，它非常有需要，也有很大的市场。 张鹏： 妍妍教授和永亮在产品、技术层面应该有很多交流。不知道你今天听到完整的产品图景，印象比较深的是什么？ 赵妍妍： 巴布这款产品我其实也见过多次，但今天完整地、从各种技术细节，听任总「十年磨一剑」地介绍下来，还是大受触动。我本身是做情感计算的，这项技术我们从 20 年前就开始做，但正如任总所说，直到大模型出现之后，它才真正能和广大 C 端用户见面。 刚才任总从很多视角讲到巴布的功能，有几个点给我留下特别深的印象。 第一是记忆功能。大家可能对发布里两个孩子、一位退休老干部的例子印象很深，我来解读一下：巴布有记忆功能，它能记住孩子的爱好，比如孩子非常喜欢地铁，它就会沿着这个爱好做语义建模，为孩子提供更好的对话和追问回应。这是「记忆+个性化回复」非常重要的技术点。 第二是实时的多模态情绪感知，这一点很让我触动，技术实现也很难得。小机器人要有追踪能力，随时追踪、随时观察，并且要从多个视角、多个通道、多种模态去观察情感，是一项挺难的技术。 第三是它能做到比较好的安全。一款产品，尤其是陪伴孩子、服务老人这样敏感人群的产品，安全格外重要——从物理安全到内容安全，再到隐私保护，都是用户购买时会担忧的地方。我们从内容安全防控、隐私计算、隐私保护等各种技术角度做了防护，让消费者能够放心。这是我印象比较深的几个技术点。 张鹏： 听起来，长期记忆加上完整的技术边界设定，让你从专业角度看到了它背后的投入和思考的周全。确实，普通消费者可能只看到某个功能，而妍妍教授能看到不一样的东西。 最满意的功能：把陪伴「编程」出来 张鹏： 那我问问永亮，如果让你挑一个到目前为止最满意的功能——其他的你肯定也喜欢，但就挑一个——巴布身上，你最想点评的是哪一点？ 任永亮： 我个人最满意的，是最后提到的报告功能。这个功能能让我像编程一样，去定义我如何陪伴孩子。这个机器人真的是一个智能体（Agent），我可以把自己的想法、孩子的反馈，用一种编程的方式实现出来。家长和孩子互动，天然会有一种对立感，这是身份带来的；但通过这样一个中间载体，我觉得很有趣。我说过，我是一个程序员。 张鹏： 接着想问问妍妍教授，人一眼就能看出对方高不高兴，但机器人要真正「懂人」，难在哪？技术上的难度阶梯是什么？ 赵妍妍： 这是一个特别好的问题。情感认知、情感计算其实分成几个层级。 第一层是情感感知。什么是感知？就是能感受到对方高兴还是不高兴。 第二层是情感认知。刚才永亮总在介绍里提到一个「事件语义」的概念，在我看来就是情感认知——我们看到一个人高兴或不高兴，会非常想知道为什么，想知道是什么事件触动了他、他不开心背后隐含着什么理由。也就是要挖掘他背后隐藏的事件。 第三层，其实就是今天巴布的形态，是情感交互。永亮总也提到，过去我们只关注语言、语音，现在开始关注实体、关注具身。交互最好的模式，就是和实体、和具身进行交互。所以更高的难度是：机器人在感知到用户不开心、并且知道背后的原因之后，能够做出更有实质性的帮扶动作，这比单纯的言语安慰要高级得多。 从情感感知、认知到交互，是层层递进的难度。 张鹏： 所以有时候，不是你设定一个所谓的模式，问题就能被有效解决。要真正精准，就像你刚才谈到的多模态——模态越丰富、上下文越充分，才越有可能有效识别。 赵妍妍： 是的，是这样。 张鹏： 这也是为什么，如果机器人不能移动、不能跟随人、不能主动看人，只是等着人来向它「汇报」，就很难。某种程度上，这也解释了永亮当时为什么跟我说要做一个可移动的机器人——我当时觉得很难，但后来认为他确实必须这么做，这也印证了技术本身就有这样的硬性要求。 赵妍妍： 是的。多模态信号的感知，不能指望人凑到一个固定的电子宠物面前让它感知，它必须具备主动感知的能力，所以跟随能力非常重要。 老龄化中国，家庭是主战场 张鹏： 技术之外，我想请贾常委给我们一些不同视角。站在整个国情的大背景下，在今天中国的家庭环境、社会环境里，机器人进入家庭，您觉得它特别值得去解决的问题是什么？它进入家庭的必要性在哪里？基于您对中国国情的全面了解，会怎么看？ 贾楠： 大家可能都知道，中国的人口结构已经发生了很大变化。截至 2025 年底，中国常住人口中 60 岁以上的已经占到 23%，相当于将近四分之一的人口都是 60 岁以上的老人；65 岁以上的老人占到 15.9%，而且这个比重还在逐年增长。 1963 年是出生人口的最高峰，有 2970 多万；1964 年、1965 年这两年也都超过 2700 万。现在这一代人已经进入退休年龄。从 1963 年之后，我国基本上每年有将近 2000 万人进入 60 岁以上，中国的老龄化问题越来越严重。 据相关部门推算，我国现在失能老人、独居老人将近 4000 多万。 对这些失能、独居老人来说，护理是非常迫切的需求。独居老人一个人在家，虽然有些生活能够自理，但一方面会寂寞，另一方面一些家务劳动也需要别人帮忙。我国目前护理人员的数量远远不够，合格的保姆、护理人员更加稀缺。 我经常去敬老院，会听到一些老人说，他们本来是想居家养老的，但因为找不到合格、称心的保姆，被迫进了敬老院。 我们也做过很多调研，中国进入老龄化社会之后，国家出台了很多政策，支持政府、企业、社会各方建设养老机构，这些确实能解决一部分养老问题。但据调查，绝大多数老人还是希望居家养老。而居家养老，随着年龄增大、自理能力越来越弱，就需要帮手。 我自己已经年近 70，周围也都是退休的朋友，大家基本都希望能有一个帮忙做家务、护理老人的智能机器人，而且更希望它是「全能」的。 张鹏： 「全能」，这是一条技术逐渐发展的路径，真要让一个机器人帮老人做家务、照顾老人，前面也得有个铺垫：先把它放在家里、放在人身边，理解人的需求和情绪，之后才能更好地在物理上服务。所以今天机器人进家庭，先瞄准理解与陪伴，是必要的一步。 贾楠： 现在的机器人功能都很单一，有的只能做饭，有的只能打扫卫生，有的只能护理病人，「全能」机器人目前还是一个理想和梦想。 另外就是与人交流。对独居老人来说，更多的是寂寞，精神上的寂寞会引发很多疾病，比如老年痴呆，就和记忆有很大关系。 刚才任总讲到，要留住老人的记忆，也不要给年轻人留下遗憾，这一点我非常有体会。我母亲已经 90 多岁，现在住在敬老院。我经常去看她、陪她聊天，她会反复聊起以前的事情，就像任总说的，可能已经听过无数遍了。一方面你没有时间坐下来听，另一方面听多了也会有厌烦情绪，这是人之常情。所以老人需要一个倾听的伙伴，这种情绪交流非常重要。 老人孤独之后很愿意回忆，从前的事，无论是美好的还是痛苦的，都希望能向人倾诉；而倾诉必须有人倾听。有巴布这样的机器人在，情绪上的陪伴非常重要。 张鹏： 所以，老人要被照顾、被关爱，这是明确的方向，技术也需要一步步爬坡。但有些问题，其实今天就可以先努力解决，比如情绪上的陪伴：多倾听、陪聊天，时不时追问几句当年的事，老人应该会很开心。 我们这代人缺的，往往是陪父母聊天的时间。今天有了巴布，可能会好一点——它可以像个小孙子，天天追着爷爷问「你当年的事」，多讲讲故事。对老人来说这是一种快乐，对我们来说也许就少一些遗憾。您刚才说的这一点，永亮未来应该把它发扬光大。 任永亮： 收到你的建议。 从感知到自进化：让机器人学会成长 张鹏： 再问问永亮，我注意到你们和哈工大的情感研究实验室有合作，我挺好奇，什么事是你搞不定、要找学界聊的？你们合作的是什么方向？ 任永亮： 我们合作的，主要是个性化对话技术，以及情感数据如何在其中起到反馈信号的作用，这是我最关心的。今天是产品发布会，我介绍的都是已经做出来的东西，很多正在做的功能没有提。 我非常强调「感知」。感知不仅是一家企业的事，它更是未来整个 AI 能力迭代最重要的输入。现在大家都在提 RSI，也就是自进化。 我们把这台机器人定位为家庭智能体，而智能体是一个 Harness（框架）工程，未来我们一定要从 Harness 进化到模型、进化到端到端——我不太愿意提这些技术名词，但这是我们最终的目标。 而进化到端到端，很难收集到足够的数据，所以我需要它在感知过程中，捕捉足够多关于人的信号、人的反馈信号，去优化内在的系统。就像人学习，我们不像大模型那样一次性把世界上所有的书都看完，而是在与人的互动中不断收获反馈、调节自己、优化自己。 我希望未来每一台巴布都具备这样的潜力，能通过情感信号去理解人真正的意图。我觉得赵教授说的「情感认知」，有一种一击即中的感觉。 张鹏： 顺着这个话题，我也想再问一下妍妍教授，被动接受任务很容易，难的是让它主动回应、让你觉得它真的是个伙伴。这个怎么才能做到？ 赵妍妍： 这个问题特别好，也确实很难实现，包括我和任总后续的很多合作，也会聚焦在这个问题上。 任何一款机器人进入家庭、与人交互，都处于一个冷启动状态。在这个过程中，它怎样越来越了解家里的每一个成员？需要我们和它不停地互动，它也在自主进化。 它对用户的了解，第一点是比较泛化的了解，也就是性格；除此之外，还要记住用户的很多喜好，比如喜欢吃什么、喜欢玩什么、习惯在哪个时间段做什么。我的想法是，怎样才能更好地读懂人？意味着我们知道他越多的事，就越知道他遇到某件事时最喜欢的反应，越了解他认知里的东西，也就更懂这个人。 所以后续我们合作要做的，就是更好地模拟各种各样的用户，从而做到更好地懂人、了解人。 张鹏： 我再追问一个更细节的点。一般要建立一个可成长的体系，都要定一个目标。比如在关系建立上，有没有一个客观的衡量角度，能够定义关系的建立和深入？ 赵妍妍： 它其实牵扯到评价。事实上，我们在了解每个用户时，需要机器人在交流的整个过程中实时监测人的反馈。 最好的评价就是人的反馈。人如果喜爱一款产品，就会乐于跟它分享更多东西、说更长的话，表情也会更愉悦。所以人在和机器人对话的过程中，反馈本身就是一种评价指征。 这也是为什么做具身、进入 C 端很重要——我们会收取大量数据，进行话术调控。比如在共情时，结合个性化和当前用户的状态，就能做更好的调控；当我发现他已经不乐意讲话了，就不要再絮絮叨叨说个不停，并不是我一直讲就是更受欢迎，及时终止，可能也是一种好的共情。就是要不停地调整状态。 一代产品的取舍，与银发经济的蓝海 张鹏： 做硬件，一代产品往往就要妥协、要取舍——想要完美，产品永远发不出来。永亮，你已经花了很长时间打磨，那么，这一代产品有哪些想做、但先放下的功能？你接下来最想推动的是什么？ 任永亮： 从大的方面讲，就像刚才贾常委提到的，「干活」肯定也是所有具身智能公司追求的目标。比如在提供情绪价值的同时，能适当地做一些家务：我们不仅能提醒老人及时吃药，也可以给老人倒一杯水、把药递到老人嘴边。这一定是一个非常长期的课题。 短期来看，就巴布这一代的形态，我觉得还有非常多的参数没有达到特别满意的状态。我们之所以把价格定得足够低，核心是想和用户交朋友，真正了解用户在使用过程中会遇到哪些问题——这是做产品最有趣的地方。也许今天的这些功能，用户一时还不敢用，但用户可能会给我提供新的需求、新的想法。 做产品，本身就是一个冒险和探索的过程。 张鹏： 再问贾常委一个我挺感兴趣的问题，怎么让老年人的市场，也能像年轻人市场一样，有一堆人抢着做好产品？ 贾楠： 现在创新能力、研发能力主要靠年轻人，而他们确实可能更关注自己的兴趣爱好和身边的人。本身是年轻人，就更容易从自我出发去研究产品。 但说到老年人，刚才也讲了，中国的老龄化社会已经非常严重，这部分的需求会越来越多、越来越广，所以年轻人确实需要投入更多的爱。这些年轻人本身也有父母，你如何对待自己的父母，就会如何去考虑老人的需求。 中国还有一个特殊现象，就是独生子女。独生子女政策各有利弊，它对控制人口起到了很好的作用，但也确实对一代人、几代人的性格成长，以及他们与社会的融合，造成了不太好的影响。所以需要年轻人更多地拓展研究思路，去关爱老年人。 我经常去养老机构、社区调研，会看到一些年轻人在从事养老事业，我就问他们为什么，他们说「热爱」。其中有些人，是从小和爷爷奶奶这一辈一起长大的，所以他们愿意去陪伴老人。 这些年轻人会从老人的需求出发，去做一些服务、做一些产品研发，这样就可能让养老、适老化的产品得到拓展。 更多的，我希望年轻人能得到一些帮助：一个是政策的优惠和引导，现在国家也在推动养老、银发经济，这是一方面。 张鹏： 其实银发经济还是一片很蓝海的市场。 贾楠： 对，是一个很大的市场。中国有这么多老年人口，需求非常强大，背后是广大的市场。我希望年轻人在更多接触上一辈老人的同时，去研究老人的需求、关爱老人。

title: This robotics concept helps explain the jaggedness of frontier capabilities
summary: The last year has seen incredible progress in model capabilities in certain domains — most notably programming , mathematics , and cybersecurity . Yet the real-world impact of these breakthroughs has been surprisingly modest — especially outside of those professions. Lawyers, architects, salespeople, college professors, and others are certainly using AI models in their work, but AI models don’t seem close to transforming those professions the way they seem to be transforming mathematics and computer programming. And even in the software industry, we’re not seeing the kind of mass unemployment many people expected we would see once AI models reached human capabilities. A big question is why — and whether the impact might grow in the next few months or years. Many people expect massive AI-driven disruptions to begin hitting other professions in 2028 or even 2027. I don’t think that’s going to happen, and a concept from robotics helps to explain why: the sim-to-real gap. I encountered this concept when I was editing my colleague Kai Williams’s excellent September article about the scramble to collect robotics training data. Suppose you want to train a robot to walk. One option is to create a virtual environment with a simulated robot.

summary: Today, I’m talking with Willy Shih, an economist, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, and the author of the upcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? Willy is one of my all-time favorite Decoder guests — his way of looking at the world through our supply chains is just a fascinating way of making sense of the global economy. I first met Willy in 2019, while The Verge was covering Foxconn’s promise to build an LCD fab in Wisconsin. summary: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself. title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
summary: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
summary: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators . Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government. summary: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. Google didn't see the backlash coming, but now that it's here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what's changing. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts. When Google revealed its new policy, the company's VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will "turn off search" if schools reject AI. summary: ChatGPT allegedly helped a North Carolina woman, Cheryl Gates, craft a “personalized plan” to poison her husband, James, after fueling her delusions that he planned to divorce her and leave her with nothing. title: Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market
summary: Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States. The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor. “When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst , co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. "Because they're paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward.” Read full article Comments

title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
summary: Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide. One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects. In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US. summary: Russian tech companies are scrambling to harden and hide their data centers underground after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged facilities housing AI supercomputers and disrupted cloud services for millions of Russian users. These consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine come as the Russian military has bombarded Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles nearly night and day in recent months, along with specifically targeting Ukrainian data centers since late September. But Ukraine has retaliated with its own drone strikes on military and infrastructure targets across Russia, degrading or knocking out data centers operated by Russian tech giant Yandex , the state-owned bank Sberbank, social media site VKontakte, and the Russian Ministry of Finance. title: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
summary: While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks , the ubiquity of these devices has made the company's education products huge in schools. Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom. However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision. Google's new overarching approach to AI in K-12 classrooms sounds good on the surface. After consulting educators, researchers, and lawmakers, Google has decided that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default. It will be up to administrators to manually enable them when these changes roll out in the coming months. When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear. The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search . There's no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it. Read full article Comments

summary: Dropbox announced Thursday plans to acquire Tigris Data for $350 million in a transaction the company told Crunchbase News would mark its largest acquisition since its founding in 2007. Founded by former Uber engineers, Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris is building a network of localized data storage centers that it claims can meet the distributed compute needs of modern AI workloads. Tigris has raised about $31.9 million since its founding in 2021, per Crunchbase data . Its October 2025 Series A brought in $25 million from lead investor Spark Capital , with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and Basis Set Ventures , which also led its seed round. Other earlier backers include General Catalyst . Co-founder and CEO Ovais Tariq told TechCrunch at the time of its Series A that the startup had grown 8x every year since its founding in November 2021. The planned deal would give Dropbox a storage platform built for developers whose applications run across multiple cloud providers. The AI-driven data center building boom is only adding to that competition for workers. Labor shortages remain the biggest cause of project delays, according to a recent survey by the Associated General Contractors of America and NCCER . Some of the technology is already at work on job sites. title: Crunchbase Data: Less Than 2% Of 2026 Venture Funding Went To Post-Election Red States
summary: For the past few decades, the vast majority of U.S. startup funding has consistently gone to companies in blue states or purple states, where Democrats control all or some statewide offices. But with Tuesday’s election results, the investment divide between blue, purple and red states has grown even more pronounced. So far this year, less than 2% of all startup investment has gone to companies in post-election red states, defined as those that will have both a Republican governor and two Republican U.S. senators. The red states’ share is much smaller than in years past due to five states shifting to purple. Of those, the largest venture hub is Texas, which shifted to purple with the election of Democratic Senator James Talarico and Governor Gina Hinojosa, followed by Ohio. This year, as of Election Day, startups in the remaining 17 red states 1 , which are home to nearly a quarter of Americans, had collectively pulled in just $8.6 billion in venture funding, with Florida, Tennessee and Utah among the largest contributors. title: The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker
summary: Methodology This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna , even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs. Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi , a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs. We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers. If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

title: Most Venture Capital Is Going To Companies That Are Founded Or Led By Billionaires
summary: The majority of U.S. venture capital nowadays goes to companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires. This is not a difficult stat to unearth. So far this year, just seven companies raised more than half of all seed- through growth-stage investment. They’re mostly familiar names: OpenAI , Anthropic , xAI (now part of SpaceX ), Anduril Industries , Databricks , Prometheus and The Boring Co. These companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year. That’s just over 50% of the U.S. seed and venture investment over the same period, per Crunchbase data. title: China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October
summary: Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek . The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion. The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding. Check out these stories: I’m Ouriel Ohayon, CEO, and Co-founder of ZenGo : a crypto wallet with unparalleled simplicity and security. We’re making a super simple and safe way for everyone to access the world of crypto, recognizing that most current options in the market do not appeal to new folks - they’re too confusing, deliver a poor user experience, and don’t always give you full control over your assets or allow you to use Web3 services. We started the company about 3 years ago as a project and launched our first version of the app 2 years ago. Six months ago, we closed our Series A funding round, raising $20 million and led by Insight Partners. As of today, ZenGo serves hundreds of thousands of customers around the world, and we’re quickly growing. Because ZenGo is a non-custodial crypto wallet, meaning it’s not centralized and it’s controlled by users, anyone can access our product, from South America to South Korea. We’re moving billions of dollars of assets for our customers. It’s been an amazing journey so far, and we’re just getting started. Why ZenGo and why now? I’ve been an entrepreneur for over 2 decades, but in the last few years, it became so clear to me that crypto would become the future technological foundation for our economies and societies. It will take a couple of decades to get there, but I was frustrated with the services and products that existed in the market so far - they were too complex, and not safe enough for most users. That’s when I knew I could help build something radically simpler, safer, and more accessible to the average person. That was the genesis of ZenGo. What s your backstory and how did you get into entrepreneurship? I’ve always been a creator: I like to work on innovative ideas and think outside of the box. I ve been playing music for longer than I can remember, and I’m a big fan of jazz, which I think of as the art of creating something out of nothing. You will get so much value growing with a small startup, and develop critical skills to employ if and when you are ready to start a company of your own. After my MBA, I quickly discovered I didn’t want to work in a large company - I didn’t like the feeling I couldn’t be creative and impactful. I wanted to become my boss, make my own mistakes, and enjoy my successes. So I’ve focused on entrepreneurship and investing for the last 20+ years. Take us through your entrepreneurial journey. How did you go from day 1 to today? Let’s start with day 0. The first thing I d say is entrepreneurship is hard. Building a company is one of the most difficult things you can do, so you should only do so if you have a passion for it. Find something you obsess over - a particular market or idea that captures your attention, to the degree you can’t think about anything else. It’s easy to find good ideas, but a massive challenge to successfully execute. Once you have an idea you’re obsessed over, it’s critical to build the right team to help you on your journey. Find co-founders and the right colleagues with complementary skills and a good amount of resilience. Building a company is the hardest thing ever. There is a reason why the startup failure rate is so high. Finding co-founders resilient to failure, tension, and stress is crucial because these are all inevitable during your entrepreneurial journey. In ZenGo’s case, we were building something the industry had never seen before: A crypto wallet safe and simple, where you can virtually never lose your funds. The problem in the industry until then was that everyone was using the same generic recipes, relying on typical public/private key cryptography and assuming it was the only way to go. You’ve probably heard about investors losing access to their bitcoin forever because they misplaced their 12-24 private key phrase. We wanted to find a better way to allow users to store and control their crypto themselves, without reliance on a centralized exchange, and without having to worry about storing private keys. We had to start from a blank page, focusing on a different type of cryptography that at first, would be much more difficult to develop, but in the mid-term, would result in a massively superior customer experience. After a year of work, we reached the level of an MVP - but a minimum viable product is very different from what I like to call an MLP: a minimum loveable product. Our initial design was slow, ugly, and unusable. It took us time to fix our code and perfect the backend - it was very difficult and we have multiple patents and IP developed around this. Eventually, we were able to move forward and focus on the user interface. It’s not easy to keep everyone motivated during such a long development marathon. As an entrepreneur, you have to be able to sell your idea to your investors, your team, and your early users. You have to remember why you’re building something important. Remind your stakeholders that everyone is contributing to something so special, so transformational, that the world will be better if it exists. But the story is not enough. Progress matters, and it’s critical to be able to create a sense of momentum with your team and your early users so everyone can see how the dream is becoming a reality. As the CEO, don’t forget to build momentum from micro-milestones that lead to a superior product, step-by-step. How are you doing today and what does the future look like? At ZenGo we optimize for one thing and one thing only: building a great product we are proud to use ourselves and share with everyone around us. Of course, we also look at growth metrics but this is not the end goal. I believe that the only thing that matters in a young company is how great the product is and if people cannot live without it. Otherwise, you’re optimizing for vanity metrics. “Growth” can easily be acquired, engineered, and faked, especially in the short term. The crypto industry (and crypto wallet industry in particular) are full of products that are popular but poorly executed. This is reflected in customer satisfaction numbers and reviews. We don’t want to be like that. We’ve optimized ZenGo around customer happiness and product quality - and customer service is incredibly important to us. Through starting the business, have you learned anything particularly helpful or advantageous? In other parts of the tech world, people are inspired by Mark Zuckerberg’s slogan “Move fast and break things.” In crypto, I’d say the near-opposite is true: patience is key. The last thing we would want to do is create an insecure environment where people could lose their funds - trust and security is critical. Our focus is finding a balance between moving cautiously while keeping pace with industry competition. In the crypto world, companies are often tempted to make quick changes to products because the ecosystem moves so quickly. We’ve landed on a balance: be patient in adopting an idea, prioritizing it, and determining it is the right direction to move, then be extremely fast in execution once the decision to adopt has been made. Most mistakes we’ve made (and have seen others in the industry make) usually stem from a reactionary need to jump on a short-term trend that might not make longer sense for the company or industry. What platform/tools do you use for your business? As I mentioned before, we’re obsessed with customer support and satisfaction. We spend a disproportionate amount of time supporting our customers and helping them when they may have questions. I’ve found this to be a secret weapon to understanding what they truly want and need, ultimately transforming happy customers into ambassadors and sometimes even employees and partners. At ZenGo, we offer in-app customer support with live agents 24/7 and require every new employee to train in delivering customer support during their first few weeks on the job. My name is Rob Bentley, and I’m a co-founder and CEO of The Jed Mahonis Group. We specialize in building best-in-class iOS and Android apps for businesses of all sizes, from funded startups to large enterprises. My business partner and I started the company right out of college by investing $250 each and are closing in on our goal of turning it into a seven-figure a year agency. We continue to be the mobile tech team of our long-standing clients like Profile by Sanford Health, Kwikly, Green Mill, and others, but here are some notable projects we’ve worked on since my business partner Tim Bornhold last wrote about us : We partnered with TurnSignl to build an on-demand tele-legal app in response to a growing cultural movement. We worked alongside the team at Little Free Library to launch an app so book lovers everywhere can find little library locations near them. Tell us about what you’ve been up to! Has the business been growing? We’ve been in business for almost 10 years, and every year has seen growth, except last year, 2021. The sales cycle for $100,000+ projects like ours is a lengthy one, often 6 to 9 to 12+ months, so it would be easy to blame 2021’s dried-up sales pipeline on the 2020 pandemic. But we spent a lot of time reflecting and found the biggest contributor to our pipeline struggle was the lack of an outbound sales process. Since starting our business, we’ve been lucky with how we’ve acquired business. It mostly came in the door without any outbound effort on our part. As we learned the hard way, this will only take you so far, and we knew we needed a focused effort on outbound sales. Initially, we didn’t have the financial means to hire a person solely focused on building our sales pipeline, so my business partner and I spread sales responsibilities amongst ourselves in the meantime. My outbound sales efforts focused on getting quick wins in the door by upselling services to current clients and forging relationships with recruiters. I spent my days pouring through job boards looking for companies needing iOS and Android expertise and reaching out to them to see if they would be interested in a C2C contract. My business partner focused on the long-term efforts of building relationships with people we wanted to do business with. In this line of business, sales aren’t closed on the first interaction. It takes some back and forth to establish trust and clear lines of communication. Having an uninterrupted and distraction-free opportunity to connect with someone is so rare these days, so he started doing Walk Talks , instead of coffee meetings and Zoom chats, to help differentiate ourselves from our competition and provide a single unique memory that is easy to recall. We also started using our podcast, Constant Variables , as a targeted method for connecting with companies we want to do business with. By inviting a key decision-maker of a targeted company to be a guest on our show, we are essentially having hour-long meetings where we learn about their company’s challenges and introduce our services. (Of course, we do this in a way that isn’t solely or slimy to keep the content of the show good, so more people will want to be guests, more people will listen to the show, and more people will get to know us. We recently surpassed 25,000 downloads and have recorded over 100 episodes!) What have been your biggest lessons learned in the last year? There is a lot of value in transparency, and it can be a competitive differentiator. We found this to be true when we published our pricing on our website. Ask any software development shop what it costs to build custom mobile apps, and the short answer you often hear is: it depends on what type of solution you need. Because of this variability, if you visit any number of software development websites, you aren t likely to find a price breakdown of services. (Trust us, we checked close to a hundred competitor sites and found only two that listed pricing). But there is some productized consistency in software development, so we added a Pricing Page to our website, breaking down the costs of: Strategizing and prototyping an app Building custom mobile software Supporting custom mobile software Current clients, prospective clients, peers, and even competitors took notice. It’s become the number one visited page on our website after our homepage and has made our sales process a lot simpler. What’s in the plans for the upcoming year, and the next 5 years? For the next year, we’re looking to grow our presence in smaller markets. As more companies become technology companies, finding technical talent is becoming increasingly competitive. One of our clients came to us because the iOS and Android expertise they needed didn’t exist in their market, so we’re targeting regions like theirs in the upper Midwest. The previous year’s outbound sales efforts between the other co-founder and myself have put us in a good spot to expand our team, and we recently hired our first Business Development Rep. With someone focused full-time on acquiring clients, we expect revenue to double in the next year or two. For the next 5 years, we want to keep doing what we do best: build strong partnerships with teams who see the value of a mobile app or web tool within the larger context of their organization. We will build and improve our processes so we can address our weaknesses and focus on delivering high-quality software as quickly as possible. We will continue to lead our industry and learn more about emerging technologies so that we can give our clients the best possible advice on how to utilize them. Have you listened to any good podcasts in the last year? Your Four Advantages Over an In-House Department by the 2BOBS Podcast talks about when agencies partner with larger organizations, they get put into one of three situations: 1) They get plugged into no existing team. 2) They get plugged into a team of 1-5 people. 3) They get plugged into a team of 6-200 people. After listening to this episode, we began thinking through our clients and their needs and realized we fit best into Situation 2, so we changed the copy on our website to resonate more with folks in organizations with existing IT teams of 1-5ish people. Our messaging became clear: “You’ve got a great IT team who doesn’t have experience in mobile. Plug us in and let us lead the way.” If you don’t have time to listen to the full 2BOBS episode, here’s a cool infographic from their website. Advice for other entrepreneurs who might be struggling to grow their business? Communication is everything. Keep in touch with your clients. Keep in touch with your team. If something feels wrong or inadequate, address it right away so it doesn’t grow and fester into resentment. In the app development industry, it’s common to hear people say, “Ideas are cheap, execution is everything.” After 10 years of running my own business, I couldn’t agree more. The concept of running a business is pretty simple: provide value to someone in exchange for money. Executing that concept, however, means different things to everybody. That’s why you see so many businesses doing the same thing but in slightly different ways. You’ve got to work with your team and clients to make sure you’re always striving to get better. My name is Kevin Miller, and I help scale the best D2C technology companies with proven growth marketing frameworks I learned at Google and various startups. I am currently the Founder of The Word Counter . As an interesting case study for my main business GR0 , an SEO agency, I went so far as to build a website that could help count words, track keywords, and even generate words from letters for games like Scrabble. It wasn’t just a fun side project -- I wanted to use the website to serve as a proof of concept and a way to put my SEO work into practice. I aimed to build an English-language online tool that was completely free to use. Our typical audience consists typically of students, copywriters, or English learning users, but the tool is available to anyone online who needs help with English or writing-related queries. In just two years, we rank for over 300,000 keywords and have over 2,400 domain referrals, and achieved 52 in domain authority. This shows how valuable and sustainable investing in SEO can be. What s your backstory and how did you come up with the idea? I grew up in Ormond Beach, FL, and I went to college at Georgetown University. Following my time in DC, I had the privilege of living in the most beautiful city in the United States, San Francisco, where I learned, lived, and breathed startups. I worked at 5 different startups you wouldn’t have ever heard of, and I worked at two companies you would, Google and Opendoor , at which I was the Head of Growth Marketing. I learned by doing, and it was painful at times, but worth it. While I was in college, I was constantly using character counter and word counter tools. I was an avid user, as were quite a few of my other classmates, however, there was no one authority on Google that was the tool to use. And understandably, since none of the tools were well-developed, easy to use, or served as the ultimate resource for all things English language. I realized there was a huge opportunity here to become that tool. At the time that I realized this opportunity, I was also honing my skills in SEO and realized that this could be the perfect case study for my strategies: a website that I would build from scratch and use only SEO tactics on from start to finish. If I could grow this website to rank #1 through solely SEO, I knew my strategies could work elsewhere too. Take us through the process of designing, prototyping, and manufacturing your first product. I wanted to build a product that was easy to use and visually appealing to the user. Although a seemingly simple task, this proved to not be the standard across the board for all of the free word-counter tools I found on Page 1 of Google. I wanted to build a product that had ease of use, and visual appeal - allowing them to clearly see words, characters, sentences, and pages since all competitors did not have that in a single view. Another goal was to build a tool that would allow the user to determine their writing’s reading level and speaking time for presentation purposes. Ultimately, I wanted to create a one-stop tool that could serve users for all logistical purposes regarding writing, as well as answer frequently asked questions regarding the English language. To do this, I hired a developer from Techy Scouts . This company was referred to me, and I have learned over several projects that the best partners to outsource work should always be through referrals from people you trust, as you have a very honest and real case study to refer to. Under my direction, Techy Scouts was able to design the product over the course of 60-90 days with very small tweaks on my end. The cost of developing the website and tool was $25,000 total, which I bootstrapped myself. I knew I wanted to monetize the site with ads, but the main intention of the site was never to be a profit source for me. I invested in this to act as a case study for my SEO tactics, and even though it was a large sum upfront, it was worth the investment regardless to be able to have tangible proof that my tactics can take a website from nothing to ranking on Page 1 of Google. I still use the site to this day as a case study for my current company GR0, and it is an invaluable resource to show potential clients. Describe the process of launching the business. While the tool was in development, we prepared for the nearing launch by getting started on our organic SEO efforts to drive traffic. Before launch, we had 100 content articles written to fill the website with meaningful and relevant content that answered questions about the English language. We did this purposefully so that it could begin to rank for multiple keywords. I also did this to make the site seem more reputable like it wasn’t brand new. I didn’t want users to visit the site and see that it was new – I wanted to give the impression that it was established. However, in terms of SEO strategy, it is more useful to publish articles consistently rather than all at once. Publishing day after day after day continuously alerts Google to check and crawl your website. If you post all at once, Google is only alerted once to go to your website, whereas posting consistently indicates to Google that your site should be crawled regularly and it builds trust in Google’s eyes. Since launch, what has worked to attract and retain customers? Since launch, we have focused solely on attracting and retaining customers through organic channels. Since this product was also built to act as a case study for my SEO tactics, I chose to focus all of my efforts on SEO. After the initial 100 articles that we prepared for launch, I also contracted writers to continue creating content at a high volume -- approximately 5 articles per business day. This is an extremely high publishing rate, and not common for most new site launches, however, I wanted to prove that writing content on related keywords could help bolster your search rankings. We put in our 10,000 hours in our keyword research to determine what questions people had about the English language. In addition, we also made it a priority to garner backlinks to increase The Word Counter’s domain authority. We accomplished this using two methods: press releases and reporter outreach. WeWorked is an easy-to-use timesheet software product that integrates invoicing, leave tracking, expense tracking, and more. WeWorked is designed specifically for small businesses in any part of the world. Most business software is designed for large enterprise customers, which results in high prices, unwanted features, a slow enhancement rate, and terrible customer service for small businesses. WeWorked focuses on the time tracking needs for small businesses by integrating leave tracking, invoices, expense tracking, and reports into an online application at an affordable price point. We are bootstrapped and profitable hosting timesheets for about 20k subscribers and average monthly revenue of $100k. Explainer video: What s your backstory and how did you come up with the idea? Growing up as a kid in inner-city Washington, DC, I always had the gut feeling that I was meant to do something big. Although I had absolutely no idea of how I was going to get there, I was 100% certain that it was to be. Hi, my name is Tyler York and I’m one of the founders of Achievable . We help people reach their target score on their most important exams. Our flagship product lines are our FINRA courses for the FINRA SIE, Series 7, Series 63, and Series 66; and our GRE exam course. We have also recently launched a USMLE Step 1 course, as well as AMC-8 and AMC-10/12 courses. We’ve more than tripled our revenue YoY in 2021! Our new GRE course was very successful and we saw continued strong growth and adoption in our FINRA business. We’re aiming even higher for 2022 and beyond. Tell us about what you’ve been up to! Has the business been growing? This year, we saw breakout growth across our FINRA and GRE courses. This growth came with zero paid marketing spend, so how did we do it? First and foremost, we benefit from having an incredibly strong product. The adoption stories are pretty fun and keep piling up. For instance, I gave my father’s friend a promo code for six free FINRA licenses for his small firm, though he told me that his students were most of the way through studying via a competitor. After a week, he called me to tell me that not only did all six students switch to Achievable, their primary question to him was “why didn’t you give this to us in the first place?” When people like the product, word gets around - especially for a painful problem like studying for these exams. This is reinforced by the fact that the majority of our traffic this year was organic, driven by some combination of word-of-mouth and our SEO efforts. Second, we saw the fruits of our strong SEO efforts to date. We spent much of 2019 and 2020 focused on building great content that served as the foundation for our SEO strategy. While it was time consuming to build this content and then work to build out relevant, high quality backlinks, the payoff is clear in the consistent, high quality organic traffic that it brings in. One of my favorite things about this is that we’re now the #1 search term for the word “Achievable” - even above the Merriam-Webster Dictionary definition for the word. Incredible! As a pair to this SEO content marketing strategy, we also put out a GRE podcast called GRE Snacks . What started as a humble experiment quickly became the #1 GRE podcast on Apple, Google, and Spotify with over 40,000 downloads in its first year. Of course, not everything worked as planned, but we made sure to learn from our experiments at each step. One we were hopeful for was our @achievable.gre Instagram channel that contains daily high-quality vocab posts. It reached almost 700 followers, but that pales in comparison to thousands of followers on Magooshgrad or other social media accounts. In general, we’ve struggled to make social work but will continue to build out a social media presence that aligns with our mission and provides quality content for viewers. What have been your biggest lessons learned in the last year? One of the key lessons we learned this past year was the power of consistency in content marketing. Our GRE Snacks podcast is just that - small, snackable episodes. We cover important topics but they’re not hour-long deep dives, they’re about 15 minutes each. Even so, we grew a cult following within the first 3-4 months, and have had viewers reach out to say that they’ve listened to every episode - some even after they finished the GRE! It’s hard (if not impossible) to build that brand loyalty with intermittent posting. For content marketing, people need to make you a part of their routine to build that consistent viewership, and following that starts to stack views. We’re striving to bring this level of consistency to the rest of our content next year. We also learned about the power of setting quantified, measurable goals and then reviewing our progress towards those goals each week. This wasn’t totally new to us, but we incorporated these goals more into our process and the results were noticeable. People are motivated to reach their goals, and checking in consistently means that you always have a sense of urgency for hitting your weekly targets. What’s in the plans for the upcoming year, and the next 5 years? In the upcoming year, our focus is on growing our existing courses’ revenue as much as possible. Rather than spread ourselves thin by adding a bunch of new courses, we want to double down on the ones that we have and focus on scaling up their market size over time. To do this, we’ll be focusing on both expanding the channels that are working for us and trying new growth avenues. One such avenue is paid to advertise, which we did not have the capital to pursue properly this year. Now that we have more capital available, we want to invest in making paid marketing work for us. The second major avenue will be driving adoption in FINRA within institutions. Wealth management firms and banks buy the majority of their FINRA test prep for their employees and do so through salespeople rather than websites. We need to work hard to understand and unlock this opportunity for us as well - once students try Achievable, they love it, but they can’t try it if their employer hasn’t heard of us yet. We want to build a great brand that conveys this message and is recognizable to anyone in the world. We have a lot of work to do to get there, but we’re excited by the opportunity in front of us. Have you read any good books in the last year? This year, I listened to the audiobook The Secrets of Sand Hill Road: Venture Capital and How To Get It by Scott Kapor at Andreessen Horowitz. For those who are new to fundraising or venture capital, it is a complete blueprint that includes not just tactics but also key context. How VCs raise money themselves, get paid, and are motivated is important and relevant to you as a founder, but I have yet to see it covered so well in other books. Even as someone with some experience in startup land and with fundraising, I found the book to be very insightful with multiple nuggets of wisdom I hadn’t come across before. Check out these stories: I’m Omar Zenhom, co-founder and CEO of WebinarNinja . I’m also the host of The $100 MBA Show , a podcast with short, bite-sized lessons on entrepreneurship and small business. Our flagship product is the WebinarNinja platform. We designed it for people who want to grow their audience (and their business) by sharing their knowledge and experience via online lessons and presentations. Most of our customers are coaches, consultants, people who have online courses, and pretty much anyone whose business model requires them to earn trust and credibility by sharing knowledge and giving their audiences consistent wins. I started as an educator. I taught at the high school and university levels and eventually moved to administration. It was a great career, but obviously, it wasn’t my path — I was side hustling the entire time, building my businesses. Never stop learning. Be insatiable for knowledge and information. I did everything on the side, from selling sneakers on arbitrage to building websites as a freelancer. But in 2012 I finally leaped, quitting my safe, stable job to go full-time into entrepreneurship. It was terrifying, but I knew it was right. My financial situation when I left education was…challenging. I had put away some savings, but the key to survival was slashing my expenses. No car, no dinners out; I had to live very lean and make every dollar (and every minute of my time) count. It was all about giving myself the runway to last long enough to succeed. It was especially tough as a 32-year-old when many of my peers were established and settled. Here I was living like an 18-year old all over again, but it’s what was necessary. It took a few tries (and some failures) but eventually, I found the flagship product that I could build a significant business around. How that happened, how I validated the product, is one of the most important things I ever learned: don’t start with the product idea. Start with the audience, learn how to serve them, and let them tell you what they need. Then build it! The “big idea” won’t come from you alone. Take us through your entrepreneurial journey. How did you go from day 1 to today? Leaving that safe, comfortable job and risking everything to build a business is scary; there’s a lot of doubt, and usually, not much proof that you can pull it off. But in my case, I had the advantage of having been side-hustled for so long. I had built businesses — nothing super-significant, but I had built and run profitable businesses at a small scale. More importantly, I had screwed up! I had failed, I had made bad decisions and learned crucial lessons the hard way. I had the privilege of being able to get a lot of reps before I made the big transition to full-time entrepreneurship. Giving up the safety net of a salary was terrifying, but later you realize those “sink or swim” moments are so pivotal. Being in those scary situations teaches you everything, and brings out your real strengths. You learn quickly how to maximize your time and your budget, to think like an entrepreneur so you can keep money coming in while plotting out your future. It takes this really strange marriage of urgency and patience to navigate that life, but in the end, those skills are what empower you to build a future of your design. I knew I wanted to serve a community of other creators and entrepreneurs, and early on I realized I had a unique advantage: my teaching experience. I watched other entrepreneurs run webinars and workshops, and sell information-based products, and they just didn’t know-how. My years in the classroom had set me up to be a uniquely qualified “teacher” in a different context. I knew I could take big scary concepts and make them learnable and digestible — but more importantly, actionable. I could offer people abilities, not just knowledge because that’s what professional teachers do. Anyone can share information, but the real value is being able to show people how to act on it. So I set about blogging and speaking and just doing everything I could to get in front of people, share value, and build that trust. Then the webinar thing happened. So I built a simple software for myself, literally just to save my own time and headaches, with no intention of selling it. But then my webinar attendees noticed. They didn’t want to be taught how to navigate the webinar thing — they wanted to not have to do it. So I put up a landing page and offered people the chance to buy into the beta version of my upcoming webinar software. I took that money and hired a freelance developer to flesh the platform out. WebinarNinja was born. Since then, we’ve followed the same process: we upgrade and improve the software, get more customers, and reinvest revenue into making it even better. We’re on our 6th version now, and there seems to be no ceiling to how much better the software can get, or how much we can grow as a company. We’re profitable, and we’ve always been profitable because we don’t believe in operating in debt. We’ve never taken on investors or loans or anything like that; WebinarNinja is 100% self-funded. They get it. Right now we have a global remote team of 25 and growing. Check out these stories: Hi, my name is Felix, and I am the co-founder and the CEO of ADPList. ADPList is a free online mentoring platform for people to find, meet and book global mentors. ADPList was established in 2020 as a list of names, to help the many designers who found themselves out of a job due to the COVID-19 pandemic. One tab in the open-source spreadsheet focused on mentoring received the most clicks, which then inspired me, and James Baduor to build this into a platform, and that’s how Amazing Design People List (ADPList) was initiated. The platform has grown organically to a network of over 3,800 mentors and 30,000 mentees, with more than 15,000 bookings from over 70 countries in only 6 months. What s your backstory and how did you get into entrepreneurship? Before getting involved in entrepreneurship, I was a Design lead at Gotrade and the Co-founder at Packdat in 2018. I completed my studies at Singapore Polytechnic but decided to pursue entrepreneurship instead of continuing my studies at the university. The drive to create and curiosity has led me to product design. Design is a space for problem-solving, and I love the challenge of practical designing anything. I started taking online design courses after school in 2019, and this passion turned into a calling for me. The consistent day-to-day showing up is what builds one’s character. I want to create purposeful products that can make this world just a little better for humanity. This ambition turns itself into venturing with purpose. Take us through your entrepreneurial journey. How did you go from day 1 to today? We first started in April 2020 at the height of the pandemic, with a Google Spreadsheet. No one believed it would work, and people thought that this was a crazy idea. “Why would someone mentor a stranger in an entirely different country?” But our mentors have proven to the world that this idea is achievable and able to support the design community people across the world. The direct impact on the mentees’ careers is just amazing! We officially launched our website in January 2021, and the global community has been expanding since then. Today we have more than 3,000 mentors and 30,000 mentees around the globe. How are you doing today and what does the future look like? At ADPList, we are on a mission to democratize mentorship for all. We believe that everyone regardless of rich or poor, connected or unconnected - should have equal access to mentorship as an education/growth resource. My name is Michael Dent and I’m the founder of PropertyData , a subscription website for property investors and developers in the UK that helps them make better-informed decisions when buying a residential property. PropertyData helps investors research local property markets, source opportunities, and do due diligence on potential purchases. I started the business in April 2017, and today it’s making $128,000 per month in recurring revenue. What s your backstory and how did you come up with the idea? In 2017 I was running a profitable ten-person web development agency, but I was tired of that business model and looking for a way to transition to building my own SaaS product. One day I was hanging out with a friend of mine and he was showing me how he was researching local property markets because he wanted to buy an investment property. To assess prices in each area, he was making a spreadsheet and manually rekeying property addresses, prices, square footage, and so on, to calculate things like the average price, average £/sqft, and typical rental yield. To a software developer mindset, this process looked silly. It was laborious, slow, and worst of all error-prone. What if he transposed two digits while keying in the data, and that led to a £100,000 mistake? I knew there must be a way to automate at least some of this analysis, and thus the idea for PropertyData was born. It’s simple: quit your job and do it! Do it while you’re young if possible before you’re married and have kids and a mortgage. I discovered that other data analytics products existed for the UK property market, but that they were all designed for big companies and cost £500/month or more, far out of reach of the UK’s typical ‘one man band’ property investor. So I decided to launch a property market data analytics tool that would cost less than £50/month, democratizing the kind of data that the big guys were using so that any property investor or developer in the UK could benefit from it. Take us through the process of designing your first product. I knew from running my web agency, where we built full-stack websites for customers, that the MVP (Minimum Viable Product) approach was the way to go. I’d spent the last 6 years telling countless customers who arrived with 60+ page technical specs to go away and come back with the smallest ‘core’ version of their idea for us to build first. So I followed my own advice and built an MVP myself in just 3 weeks, all the while continuing to manage my agency. The MVP was simple – it enabled users to define a custom area, and then connect to the API of Zoopla, a major UK property portal, and ran an analysis of the local property market in that area. The clever bit was a piece of code that used OCR technology to read the internal area of a property from the floorplan and then calculated the £/sqft. It didn’t cost me a penny (other than my time) to finish the MVP, and I soon had it up and running on a $5/month cloud instance. The joys of starting a business in the era of cheap cloud computing! Describe the process of launching the business. I cobbled together a press release and sent it to a few industry news sites. One or two took the bait. A guy called Nick who runs London’s biggest property trade show saw one of the articles and called me and asked me if I wanted to take a last-minute stand at a good rate, with just a week to prepare. In some ways, it seemed like an old-fashioned way to promote a software product, but I knew it would get me in front of potential customers who would ask hard questions, and it would be a great way to test product-market fit. Pricing was something I wasn’t sure about, but I knew I did want the price to be an obstacle to early traction, so I set the first pricing very low with three packages at £6, £12, and £24 per month. I thought it would be easy to raise prices later for new users, which in due course I did. Iterate constantly - deploy new features every week if not every day, guided by both user suggestions and your own vision So I conscripted one of my agency team members to support me running the stand, and off we went. Most stands had expensive and flashy fit-out, but ours was just in black ‘shell’ condition with one table with an iMac on for demos. I’ve wondered whether people were actually drawn to the simplicity of our stand, perhaps thinking that suck stark minimalism in the sea of bling must mean there might be substance to our product. We saw hundreds of people over two days, and the early reaction was very positive. We signed up a bunch of people to our mailing list and got our first subscriber in the following days. More helpful were the questions people asked. “This is cool, but can it do X?”. Which it invariably couldn’t. So I came away armed with the next 6 months worth of feature development. I felt I must be on to something, so I borrowed £50,000 from my sister so that I could close down my agency and focus full-time on PropertyData. I basically lived on that money for a year, investing all the revenue into growing the business. PropertyData has grown largely by word of mouth and referral, but of course, paid media has played a part too. Initially, I ran the Google Ads campaigns myself, but I quickly realized this wasn’t something I was good at. I’d met a guy at a party who ran a PPC agency , so I appointed them to run Google Ads (and then Facebook/Instagram, Microsoft and LinkedIn) and never looked back. They grew the number of conversions from the campaigns consistently month-on-month for a couple of years. In the early years I structured the fee according to the number of signups they generated, which helped keep incentives aligned. We also launched a simple but generous affiliate program, which has been a steady performer delivering 5-10% of new signups and making great recurring revenue for 20-25 affiliates. The affiliates promote PropertyData however they can, most often through YouTube videos, in-person events, and their own networks. They generally create their own promotional material which I approve, and they receive a generous 25% lifetime commission on all revenue from users they refer. How are you doing today and what does the future look like? PropertyData has grown every month since launch, even through the Covid pandemic. If you're interested in reading how they got started, published about 7 years ago, check it out here. Hello again! Remind us who you are and what business you started. My name is Patrick Hess and I own a company called AFH Media LLC , a small website development and holding company. Our focus is on website acquisitions and growth strategies. I was originally featured on your site because I developed a website called bargames101.com , which I ultimately sold to another investor. Tell us about what you’ve been up to! Has the business been growing? After selling the bar games site, I built a couple of new sites and invested in a smaller affiliate site with the goal of scaling and, hopefully, flipping it. After redesigning that site and ramping up the content and SEO strategy, I increased affiliate revenue from a few hundred dollars to 5 figures a month. As mentioned, try to keep it simple and focus on one or two projects at a time. If you’re building websites as a side income stream (like me), don’t get discouraged if you don’t see immediate results. After one year, I sold that affiliate site to a large ecommerce group for a very nice exit. This might sound ridiculous, but when factoring in the purchase cost, content, and other miscellaneous costs, my ultimate ROI, including monthly revenue and sale price, was close to 2000%. Here’s a screenshot showing the results of scaling content and applying SEO strategies - you can see the initial curve after I purchased the site in late summer 2020: What have been your biggest lessons learned in the last year? Although I had some success with building and selling sites, I’ve had my share of failed projects as well. I’ve learned that this usually comes down to starting too many projects at once and being impatient. If you’re on your own (like me) and/or have limited time and resources to devote to these projects, it’s best to just focus on one or two at first. The idea of owning several sites and building your own online empire or portfolio sounds glamorous, but in reality, this is incredibly hard to achieve without a team and resources. It’s much better, in my experience, to focus on one or two projects at first. Make something great that stands out among all the over-optimized and shady sites out there. It’s worth the effort. Also, don’t be too quick to sell. I made the mistake of selling one of my first sites several years ago because I wasn’t sure it was worth the effort and wanted to cash out. I was new to the process and sold for a small amount. I built that site from scratch and wrote all the content. It was a ton of work. Now, in the hands of new owners, that site is a hugely successful affiliate site in the water sports niche. It would have been great to have held on to it a little longer, but I learned a lot from the experience. Finally, I’ve recently focused more on outsourcing and delegating certain aspects of the business. For example, I’m terrible at building links, so I found a group that excels at white hat link building. I’ve also worked with many writers and now even work with a content manager to assign topics and assist with the overall content workflow. This allows me to focus on tasks that I enjoy the most (i.e. keyword research, content planning, and design). I’m still working on this, but can definitely see the upside to delegating more and removing bottlenecks. What’s in the plans for the upcoming year, and the next 5 years? I recently invested in a couple of smaller sites and my plan is to improve the design, content quality, and SEO strategy on these. I look for sites in high-growth niches with branding potential and immediate monetization channels (i.e. affiliate marketing and display ads). Then I try to scale them with a series of articles and topic clusters. Working on one or two at a time, I hope to have a handful of successful content sites over the next few years that generate consistent monthly revenue with solid exit potential. He covers the central teachings of several famous philosophers, but manages to keep it light and funny. It’s a great book to revisit from time to time. Advice for other entrepreneurs who might be struggling to grow their business? As mentioned, try to keep it simple and focus on one or two projects at a time. If you’re building websites as a side income stream (like me), don’t get discouraged if you don’t see immediate results. It takes a while, especially if you’re starting from scratch. In the meantime, focus on quality, make something that stands out from the crowd, and learn all about keyword research, on-page SEO, WordPress, content marketing and site structure.
